rationale: Both candidates are near-clones: same angina pectoris PheCode 411.3 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same method (LDpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distributions, and same validation size (n=30,750). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model C-index is shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric. With everything else effectively identical, PGS005048 has a trivially higher full-model C-index (0.76688 vs 0.76625), so it edges PGS005052 on the only differentiating field, but the difference is essentially noise—hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation N (24,905), so endpoint/design evidence is essentially tied. Candidate_a (PGS001261) has slightly better PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.58233 vs 0.58108; PGS-only R2 0.01228 vs 0.01185; incremental AUROC 0.00796 vs 0.00783) and also a more explicit endpoint description aligned to the target (‘Angina pectoris (time-to-event)’ / ‘TTE angina pectoris’) than candidate_b’s more generic ‘Angina’. Differences are small, hence low confidence, but they consistently favor PGS001261.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS000753 is from a disease-focused AAA genetics study (Million Veteran Program; Circulation) with a clearly stated clinical endpoint (“Prevalent abdominal aortic aneurysm”) and provides a directly interpretable PRS effect size (OR per SD = 1.37, moderate discrimination signal). PGS002054 comes from a UKB portability/framework paper (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) and only reports a weak PRS-comparable metric (partial-r = 0.0144) with no OR/HR/AUC/R2, making its evidence for AAA-specific predictive utility thinner despite the larger genome-wide LDpred2 construction and larger training N. Given domain guidance that disease-focused models typically outperform portability-framework scores unless the framework has clearly stronger endpoint+metric evidence, PGS000753 is better supported here.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS003972 is better supported by study archetype and development context: it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many contributing cohorts listed) using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with broader GWAS ancestry (AFR+EUR) and very large variant coverage (~1.12M). In contrast, PGS002054 is from a UKB portability framework paper (single-cohort development, LDpred2) with only a weak PRS signal reported (partial-r=0.0144) and no direct discrimination metric; despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation and larger validation N, framework-origin and modest metric evidence make it less compelling than the disease-focused meta-analysis score.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper, with identical covariates (age/sex/array/PCs) and similar ancestry setup (EUR development; multi-ancestry evaluation listed but selected European validation). The main differentiators are endpoint framing and PRS-only performance: PGS001262 uses a direct doctor-diagnosed angina phenotype (better aligned to generic angina pectoris than the time-to-event packaging in PGS001261, which is a mild endpoint-fidelity negative per guidance), and it has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC (0.5868 vs 0.5823) and PRS-only R² (0.0130 vs 0.0123), both well below the heritability ceiling so plausible. Although PGS001261 has more variants and larger training N, those are weaker signals here and don’t outweigh PGS001262’s cleaner endpoint and marginally better PRS-only metrics.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both "Alcohol use disorder" and trait_efo maps to "alcohol dependence." It also shows stronger PRS signal evidence via an OR top 10% vs rest of 1.96 (1.54–2.51), which is a meaningful discriminative effect size. In contrast, PGS000202 is less endpoint-faithful (trait_reported is "Problematic alcohol use" and trait_efo is a measurement construct), and its reported incremental ΔR² is small (0.00456) with a modest beta (0.043). Both lack clean PRS-only AUC/R², so the decision leans on phenotype fidelity and effect-size strength, favoring PGS002738 despite its unknown covariates.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and use only basic demographic/PC covariates (no obvious clinical-risk packaging). PGS001784 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.014661, which is interpretable and below the trait heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.02), whereas PGS002054 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and only provides a partial correlation (0.0144), a less standard and less directly comparable metric. Additionally, PGS001784 is developed across multiple biobanks (global biobank framework) with a larger EUR evaluation sample (n=350,767) than PGS002054’s UKB-only evaluation (n=19,545), giving more robust validation context despite both being framework-style papers.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported = abdominal aortic aneurysm), same method (PRS-CS), same variant count, same GWAS/eval ancestry mix (EUR eval), and same publication/date—so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the only performance numbers shown are full-model metrics and are not clean PRS-comparable; however, candidate_a (PGS003973) at least discloses basic demographic covariates (age, age^2, sex), making its reported C-index=0.882 more interpretable as a covariate-adjusted model, whereas candidate_b (PGS003972) has covariates listed as Unknown and a lower full-model AUROC=0.69. With otherwise indistinguishable metadata, the combination of clearer covariate specification and stronger (albeit full-model) discrimination favors PGS003973.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo=angina pectoris; phenotyping_reported is angina/angina pectoris), but PGS001260 provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.581 and PGS-only R²=0.01185) with basic covariates and an R² that is plausible under the trait’s low observed h² ceiling. In contrast, PGS005048 reports only a full-model C-index (0.767) plus an OR=1.487, with no PGS-only AUC/R²; per the guidance, the full-model metric is not a valid substitute for PRS discrimination, making its PRS strength less directly supported despite its genome-wide method/variant count and diverse-populations framing. Therefore the better-supported record on visible PRS evidence is PGS001260.

PGS000201 is the better-supported match to the target concept despite its less exact surface label: its phenotyping_reported is an AUD DSM-5 criteria count (directly on the alcohol dependence/AUD spectrum) with clearly stated basic covariates, and it uses a genome-wide PRS-CS score (1,094,954 variants), which is structurally appropriate for a polygenic trait. PGS002739 has very good endpoint fidelity (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=alcohol use disorder) and provides a useful risk-stratification metric (OR top 10% vs rest=1.76), but it is evaluated only in AFR and is a very sparse gene-based score (858 variants) with covariates listed as unknown, making its standalone PRS evidence and comparability less clear. With neither candidate reporting PRS-only AUC/R2, the stronger structural genome-wide model plus clearer covariate disclosure favors PGS000201.

Both candidates align to angina pectoris by trait_efo, but PGS005048 has higher endpoint fidelity via a diagnosis-code definition (PheCode 411.3) and comes from a disease-focused diverse-populations PRS methods comparison using MVP with multi-ancestry GWAS/evaluation and a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.487, near the ≥1.5 strong-signal guideline). In contrast, PGS001262 is a UK Biobank pan-trait sparse-framework score (“across 813 traits”) with modest PRS-only performance (AUROC 0.5868; R2 0.0130) and the very high full-model AUROC is largely covariate-driven (incremental AUROC only 0.0098), consistent with the heritability-ceiling sanity check. Although PGS001262 reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, the framework-study penalty plus weaker PRS signal makes PGS005048 better-supported overall.

PGS004913 is the better-supported match to the target endpoint: its trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both directly specify alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis, aligning cleanly with the target trait, and it reports a PRS effect size (OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4) with basic, non-leaky covariates (age/sex/PCs) and explicit training+validation sample sizes. PGS001777 has a relevant trait_reported but its phenotyping_reported is less endpoint-faithful ("Cirrhosis (males)") and its only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC (0.671) with unknown covariates, which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven; it also lacks training sample size details and appears more like a small 3-variant risk score packaged with non-genetic predictors (per title).

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and both are evaluated in EUR. However, PGS001784 comes from a pan-trait/global-biobank framework paper ("Global Biobank analyses...") and uses a heavier covariate set (age/sex interactions + 20 PCs), and its only PRS-comparable metric is a modest covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.014661 (below the h2_liability ceiling 0.02, but not clearly strong). PGS003973 is from a disease-focused AAA GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet; many AAA-relevant cohorts including MVP, eMERGE, deCODE, etc.) with basic covariates (age, age^2, sex) and a larger genome-wide PRS (1.12M variants vs 0.91M). Although PGS003973 lacks an explicit PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model C-index 0.882, not directly comparable), the stronger disease-focused study archetype and cleaner covariate design outweigh PGS001784’s modest PRS-only R2 advantage.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication, method (PRS-CS), EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, same trait_reported/trait_efo, and same phenotyping_reported (DSM-5 AUD criteria count, log-transformed), so endpoint fidelity to alcohol dependence is essentially identical. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are the PRS contribution metrics and supporting evidence: PGS000201 shows a larger incremental ΔR² vs covariates (0.01192 vs 0.00456) and a stronger effect size (β=0.099, SE=0.01 vs β=0.043, SE=0.019), consistent with a stronger PRS signal. PGS000201 also has slightly more variants and includes standard technical covariates (array, site) rather than being more clinically packaged. Although PGS000202 has a larger validation n (1,251 vs 7,599 is actually smaller), it does not offset the weaker PRS signal; thus PGS000201 is better-supported.

PGS005052 is better supported for angina pectoris because it uses a direct diagnosis-style endpoint (PheCode 411.3; phenotyping_reported: Angina pectoris) and comes from a disease-focused multi-population PRS methods paper with MVP development and multi-ancestry GWAS/evaluation context, plus it reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.491, near the ≥1.5 “strong” guideline). In contrast, PGS001261 is from a pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event phenotype (TTE), which domain guidance flags as a weaker archetype for external reliability; its PRS-only metrics are clean but modest (PGS-only AUROC 0.582, R2 0.0123) and the high full-model AUROC is largely covariate-driven (incremental AUROC 0.008). Overall, PGS005052 has stronger endpoint fidelity and more convincing PRS signal evidence than the framework TTE score, despite lacking explicit PGS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and neither provides a clean PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS003973 is better supported by study archetype and model construction: it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many contributing cohorts) with basic covariates (age, age^2, sex) and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with larger variant coverage (~1.12M). PGS002054 is from a UK Biobank portability/framework paper (single-cohort development) with heavier adjustment (age, sex, birth date, deprivation, 16 PCs) and only a weak PRS-comparable metric (partial-r=0.0144), which provides limited evidence of meaningful PRS signal. Although PGS002054 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation, the framework origin plus weak metric makes it less compelling than the disease-focused multi-cohort score.

Both candidates align well to the target endpoint (trait_efo alcoholic liver cirrhosis; phenotyping_reported matches: “Alcoholic cirrhosis” for PGS000704 vs “Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis” for PGS004913). However, PGS004913 is a disease-focused PRS explicitly developed for alcohol-associated cirrhosis (heavy drinkers) and provides PRS-relevant effect evidence (top vs bottom decile OR=4.4; R²=0.029), whereas PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics paper and only reports a full-model C-index/AUC=0.711 plus a modest HR=1.18, with no PRS-only AUC/R² (so its discrimination is likely largely covariate-driven and not directly comparable). Despite PGS000704’s much larger training/validation sizes and more variants, the endpoint-focused study archetype and stronger PRS-linked effect evidence make PGS004913 better-supported for alcoholic liver cirrhosis.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array etc.), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are essentially tied. PGS001267 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.7265 and PGS-only R2=0.0988 in Europeans, whereas PGS002089 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919), which is less directly interpretable for discrimination. Although PGS002089 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants (LDpred2, 22,026) versus PGS001267’s very sparse 10-variant snpnet model (a structural plus for PGS002089), the absence of comparable PRS-only metrics for PGS002089 makes its empirical support weaker here; PGS001267 also has a larger validation sample (67,425 vs 18,262).

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with identical ancestry distribution, covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), and the same mapped EFO trait (angina pectoris), so the decision rests on endpoint fidelity and PRS-only metrics. PGS001262’s phenotyping_reported/trait_reported explicitly matches the doctor-diagnosed UKB field (“Vascular/heart problems diagnosed by doctor Angina”), which is at least as endpoint-faithful as PGS001260’s generic “Angina” label. On comparable PRS-only performance, PGS001262 is slightly stronger (PGS-only AUROC 0.58683 vs 0.58108; PGS-only R² 0.01304 vs 0.01185), and both are plausible under the provided heritability ceiling. PGS001260 has larger training N and more variants, but those are weaker differentiators here given the same study archetype and the small metric gap; overall the cleaner diagnosis-anchored phenotype plus marginally better PRS-only metrics favors PGS001262.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858 for PGS002739’s gene-based PRS-CSx), which is generally a stronger structural signal for a polygenic disorder when comparable PRS-only metrics are absent. Its reported discrimination proxy is also slightly stronger (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 vs 1.76). PGS002739 has a valuable AFR-only evaluation context, but that ancestry-specific focus and smaller SNP set do not outweigh PGS002738’s stronger genome-wide construction and effect-size evidence for the generic alcohol dependence target.

PGS002738 is the better match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is explicitly Alcohol use disorder with trait_efo mapped directly to alcohol dependence, whereas PGS000201 is for “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo “alcohol dependence measurement” and a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is more of a quantitative/problem-use measure than a direct dependence diagnosis. Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared on the preferred metrics; in that setting, PGS002738 has stronger discriminative evidence via OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96 (stronger signal) compared with PGS000201’s small ΔR²=0.01192 and modest beta. PGS002738 is also developed from a broader disease-focused cohort set (MVP + UKB) versus UKB-only for PGS000201, with similar EUR-only evaluation sizes, making PGS002738 overall better-supported for the dependence/AUD target.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS003972 is better supported structurally and by study context: it is a disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis (many listed cohorts) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is generally a stronger PRS construction signal than PGS000753’s sparse P+T score with 29 variants. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS003972’s full-model AUROC=0.69 cannot be treated as a PRS-comparable advantage; however, PGS000753’s only quantitative evidence is a moderate OR=1.37 per SD and it is explicitly a prevalent endpoint, which is slightly less ideal than the generic AAA endpoint in PGS003972. Covariates are cleaner/known for PGS000753 (age/sex/PCs) versus unknown for PGS003972, which tempers confidence, but overall the method/variant coverage and broader disease-meta-analysis development make PGS003972 the stronger-supported candidate.

Both candidates align to angina pectoris (EFO match), but PGS005052 uses a direct diagnostic-code endpoint (PheCode 411.3) and comes from an MVP-based, diverse-populations PRS methods comparison context, with a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.491, ~moderate-to-strong). In contrast, PGS001262 is a UK Biobank pan-trait sparse-model score (“across 813 traits” framework) with modest PRS-only performance (AUROC 0.5868; R2 0.0130) and known generalization concerns for this study archetype; its high full-model AUROC is largely covariate-driven (incremental AUROC 0.0098). PGS005052 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, lowering certainty, but its endpoint fidelity plus stronger effect-size evidence and less framework-like origin outweigh PGS001262’s cleaner-but-weak PRS-only metrics.

PGS000704 is better supported as a standalone PRS for alcoholic liver cirrhosis: it has strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both explicitly “Alcoholic cirrhosis”), a much more polygenic genome-wide model (183,271 variants; snpnet multi-PRS) with large-scale UKB development (n=223,327) and large validation (n=135,300) plus some cross-ancestry evaluation (EUR/MAE). PGS001777 is disease-focused but is essentially a 3-variant risk score from a small evaluation (n=1,390) and its publication framing (“genetic risk score and diabetes”) suggests potential clinical-risk packaging; covariates are unknown and phenotyping_reported is partially mismatched (“Cirrhosis (males)”). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUC difference (0.711 vs 0.671) is not decisive; structural/model-scale and endpoint coherence favor PGS000704.

Both candidates match the target trait and have acceptable endpoint fidelity (PGS000753: prevalent AAA; PGS001784: AAA). However, PGS001784 is from a pan-trait/global biobank framework paper, which domain guidance penalizes versus a disease-focused AAA-specific study unless the framework score has clearly superior PRS-comparable evidence. While PGS001784 reports a PRS-comparable Nagelkerke R2 (covariates regressed out) of 0.0147 (below the ~0.02 liability h2 ceiling, so plausible), it lacks an effect-size summary and its very high AUROC (0.868) is full-model and not PRS-only. PGS000753, from an AAA-focused MVP study, provides a direct PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.37, moderate signal) with basic covariates and a clearer disease-specific development context; despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2, the disease-focused archetype plus interpretable OR outweighs the framework model’s modest R2 advantage.

Both candidates align to the target trait (trait_efo=angina pectoris), but PGS005052 has stronger endpoint specificity (PheCode 411.3 angina pectoris) and comes from a disease-focused PRS-methods comparison in diverse populations with MVP development and multi-ancestry evaluation. Although PGS005052 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.491, near the ≥1.5 ‘strong’ guideline), which is meaningful PRS evidence. PGS001260 provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.581, R2=0.01185) that are heritability-plausible, but it is from the known pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse framework (snpnet, 2562 variants), which domain guidance flags as typically less reliable for external generalization; its PRS-only discrimination is also modest. Net: PGS005052’s disease-anchored phecode endpoint + stronger effect-size signal and multi-ancestry context outweigh PGS001260’s cleaner but weak PRS-only AUROC/R2 from a framework score.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and both are evaluated in EUR. However, PGS001784 comes from a clear portability/framework-style paper (“Global Biobank analyses… across diverse cohorts”), which domain guidance penalizes versus a disease-focused AAA GWAS meta-analysis score when endpoint fidelity is otherwise similar. Its very high reported AUROC (0.868) is a full-model metric alongside basic covariates, while its PRS-comparable signal is modest (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.014661), suggesting the AUROC is largely covariate-driven; the R2 is also below the local h2_liability ceiling (~0.02), consistent with a limited PRS contribution. PGS003972 is from an AAA-specific Nat Genet meta-analysis with broader disease-focused multi-cohort development and a larger genome-wide PRS-CS model (1,118,997 variants vs 911,440), which is a positive structural signal when PRS-only metrics are not available. Given the framework penalty and the modest PRS-only R2 for PGS001784, PGS003972 is better-supported overall despite lacking a clean PRS-only metric.

Both candidates map cleanly to angina pectoris (same trait_efo), but PGS001261 is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse snpnet score with a time-to-event phenotype and modest PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.582, R2 0.0123), consistent with weak standalone PRS signal despite a higher full-model AUROC driven largely by covariates (incremental AUROC only 0.008). PGS005048 uses a disease-endpoint PheCode definition (411.3) and a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred) with far broader variant coverage (~1.29M) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.487, near the ‘strong’ threshold), which is meaningful PRS evidence even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided and its full-model C-index is not PRS-comparable. Given the framework-penalty and weak PRS-only metrics for PGS001261 versus the stronger structural/effect-size evidence for PGS005048, PGS005048 is better supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait sparse snpnet framework paper (same training cohort/size, covariates, variant count=10, and identical ancestry distribution/validation size), so the main differentiator is endpoint fidelity. PGS001267 targets a straightforward ankylosing spondylitis case-control phenotype (phenotyping_reported: "Ankylosing spondylitis"), which better matches the generic target trait than PGS001268’s time-to-event formulation ("TTE ankylosing spondylitis"), which is a mild endpoint mismatch per the provided guidance. Although PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.7346/0.1023 vs 0.7265/0.0988), the gap is small and does not outweigh the cleaner endpoint alignment of PGS001267; both R² values remain well below the heritability ceiling, so neither has a sanity-check advantage.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping all ankylosing spondylitis), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), evaluation ancestries (same EUR/GME/SAS mix) and validation N (n=18,262), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiator is performance and structure: PGS002089 shows higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0919 vs 0.0797 for PGS001876) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (22,026 vs 85), which is a positive structural signal when other fields are effectively identical. Hence PGS002089 is better supported overall.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ankylosing spondylitis), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS003420’s only visible discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.7886 with covariates listed as Unknown, which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven; it also has limited support (single record, small validation n=1,298) and a very sparse 100-variant score. PGS002089, while coming from a UKB portability framework paper, has stronger structural and support signals: genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2) with 22,026 variants, explicit basic covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), much larger validation (n=18,262) and multi-ancestry evaluation (EUR/GME/SAS), plus a PRS-comparable partial correlation reported (partial-r=0.0919). Overall, PGS002089 is better-supported on comparable PRS evidence and robustness context than PGS003420’s non-comparable full-model AUROC.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis because its concept fields align directly (trait_reported="Aortic stenosis", trait_efo="aortic stenosis") whereas PGS005255 is primarily a valve-function/measurement trait (trait_reported="Mean pressure gradient", trait_efo includes "aortic measurement"), making it less endpoint-faithful despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported (incident aortic stenosis). Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, PRS-CS, EUR-only dev/eval, same covariates, same validation N, no PRS-only AUC/R2), so the tie-breakers favor PGS005254’s stronger effect-size evidence (HR 1.64 vs 1.53) and larger training sample (205,483 vs 98,645).

PGS005254 is an exact match to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo = aortic stenosis; phenotyping_reported = incident aortic stenosis), whereas PGS004911 targets a different disease entirely (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (MTAG); phenotyping_reported = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), making it endpoint-mismatched for aortic stenosis. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004911’s reported AUROC=0.8 and R²=0.048 are full-model/non-PRS-comparable and cannot outweigh the phenotype mismatch. PGS005254 also provides a strong PRS-relevant effect size (HR per SD 1.64 with CI), supporting discriminative signal on the correct endpoint, with basic covariates and large EUR validation.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are UKB-based framework/portability-style scores, so phenotype fidelity and study archetype do not separate them. PGS001267 provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.7265; PGS-only R2=0.0988) with only basic covariates, and the PRS-only R2 is plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.399), making the performance evidence interpretable. PGS001876 reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0797) and lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, leaving weaker, less directly comparable performance support despite a larger training N and more variants. Therefore PGS001267 is better-supported on the visible record fields.

PGS002089 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait “ankylosing spondylitis” because its endpoint fidelity is a direct disease phenotype (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both ankylosing spondylitis), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) formulation (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)”), which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS001268 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346; PGS-only R2 0.10232), it comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 10-variant model (snpnet), a known generalization risk pattern; by contrast PGS002089 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (22,026) and is explicitly framed around portability, with multi-ancestry evaluation including EUR/SAS/GME. Overall, the combination of better endpoint match and stronger structural PRS construction outweighs PGS001268’s metric completeness in this head-to-head.

PGS001268 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and evaluation breadth: it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.7346; PGS R²(no covariates)=0.10232) with basic covariates and a larger validation sample (n=67,425) plus multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). PGS001876 has an endpoint-aligned label but provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0797) and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its predictive evidence less directly comparable; its evaluation is narrower and validation smaller (n=18,262). While PGS001268’s time-to-event phenotyping and pan-trait framework origin are mild negatives, the presence of explicit PRS-only metrics and broader evaluation support outweigh PGS001876’s missing PRS-comparable discrimination metrics here.

PGS001135 has clearly comparable PRS-only performance reported for the arthritis endpoint (PGS-only AUROC=0.539 and PGS-only R2=0.00291 with basic covariates listed), allowing a sanity check against the trait heritability ceiling and indicating a weak-but-quantified PRS signal. PGS004477 is closer to a specific ICD10 block label (“M13 Other arthritis”) and uses a genome-wide LDpred2 score with many variants, but it provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and has unknown covariates, leaving only a modest OR=1.20 as performance evidence. Given the lack of directly comparable metrics and covariate transparency for PGS004477, the better-supported record on visible fields is PGS001135 despite its pan-trait UKB framework origin.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis because its concept alignment is exact (trait_reported and trait_efo both aortic stenosis), whereas PGS005256 is primarily labeled as aortic valve function (trait_reported: Peak aortic velocity; trait_efo includes aortic measurement), making it a more indirect construct despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported (incident aortic stenosis). Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, PRS-CS, EUR-only dev/eval, same covariates, same validation N=244,450, no PRS-only AUC/R2), so the tie-breakers are endpoint fidelity and available effect-size strength; PGS005254 also shows a slightly stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53).

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it has exact trait alignment (trait_reported and trait_efo both aortic stenosis) and endpoint fidelity (incident aortic stenosis cases). It also shows stronger PRS signal via effect size (HR=1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255). Although PGS005252 reports only a full-model C-index/AUC (0.87) that is likely covariate-influenced given its heavy clinical covariate set, PGS005255 provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 either, so metrics don’t cleanly favor it. PGS005255 is additionally less endpoint-faithful on the surface (trait_reported is mean pressure gradient; trait_efo includes aortic measurement), making it more of a valve-function/measurement score despite mentioning incident AS in phenotyping. With both evaluated in EUR only and similar genome-wide variant counts, the stronger endpoint match and higher HR make PGS005252 the stronger choice.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence for the broad target trait “arthritis”: it reports clean PGS-only metrics (AUROC 0.539 and PGS-only R² 0.00291) with basic covariates and these are sanity-consistent with the provided low heritability ceiling context, whereas PGS004547 provides no AUROC/R² at all (only an OR=1.262, which is weak-to-moderate) and has unknown covariates. Although PGS004547 uses a more complex/meta-PRS method with far more variants and a larger EUR validation sample, its study framing (“risk factor PRS integration”) plus missing comparable metrics makes its standalone PRS quality less directly supported than PGS001135’s explicitly reported PRS-only performance.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo aortic stenosis; incident phenotyping; EUR-only dev/eval) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on effect-size evidence and comparability. PGS005252 shows a stronger PRS association (HR=1.92 vs 1.64 for PGS005254) and provides a concrete discrimination metric (C-index/full-model 0.87), whereas PGS005254 provides only the HR. Although PGS005252 uses heavier clinical covariates (multiple comorbidities/risk factors) making its full-model C-index less PRS-comparable, the stronger per-SD HR is still supportive of better PRS signal than PGS005254, and other fields (ancestry, endpoint, variant count) are essentially tied.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait aortic stenosis: same publication, same method (PRS-CS), same variant count (1,111,632), same EUR-only development/evaluation, identical covariates (age/age^2/sex/PCs), identical validation size (n=244,450), and both use the endpoint-relevant phenotyping_reported of incident aortic stenosis. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics can’t separate them; effect sizes are essentially identical (HR 1.53 for both, overlapping CIs). With no substantive differentiator, PGS005255 gets a slight edge only from marginally larger training sample (98,645 vs 96,385) and weak prior for candidate_a ordering.

PGS005255 is endpoint-aligned to the target trait aortic stenosis via phenotyping_reported="incident aortic stenosis" and trait_efo including aortic stenosis, whereas PGS004911 targets a different disease (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) in all phenotype fields and is therefore a poor match for aortic stenosis. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS004911’s reported AUROC=0.8 is a full-model metric and not comparable as PRS evidence, while PGS005255 at least provides a relevant effect size (HR=1.53) for aortic stenosis risk. With similar basic covariates and EUR-only evaluation, phenotype fidelity dominates, making PGS005255 clearly better-supported for aortic stenosis.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ankylosing spondylitis). However, PGS001876 comes from a UKB portability/framework-style paper and reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0797) with no PRS-only AUC/R2, which is relatively weak and not directly interpretable as discrimination. PGS003420 is disease-focused (Taiwanese AS GWAS) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS), and it provides an explicit AUROC=0.7886 (though it is full-model and covariates are unknown, so it cannot be treated as PRS-only). Given the framework penalty on PGS001876 and the more disease-specific development plus stronger (albeit full-model) performance signal for PGS003420, PGS003420 is better supported on the visible fields despite its smaller, single-ancestry EAS validation.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis) mapped to EFO arthritis, same publication, same UKB training cohort, identical training (n=174,489) and validation size (n=56,192), identical EUR-only development/evaluation, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR reported). With metrics and design otherwise indistinguishable, the main differentiator is the available PRS effect size: PGS004547 reports a higher OR (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), suggesting stronger PRS discrimination. Method_name also weakly favors PGS004547 (RFDiseasemetaPRS implies an aggregated/meta-PRS structure) over PGS004477 (single-score LDpred2) given the domain guidance that multi-score aggregation tends to outperform single-score construction.

PGS005256 is endpoint-aligned to the target trait aortic stenosis via phenotyping_reported="incident aortic stenosis" and trait_efo including "aortic stenosis", whereas PGS004911 targets a different disease entity (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) in trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported and thus has poor phenotype fidelity for aortic stenosis. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS004911’s reported AUROC=0.8 and R²=0.048 are full-model/non-PRS-comparable and cannot compensate for the endpoint mismatch. PGS005256 also shows supportive PRS signal for the correct endpoint (HR per SD 1.53 with CI 1.41–1.67) and uses only basic covariates, making it the better-supported choice for aortic stenosis despite lacking AUC/R2.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it is explicitly labeled and mapped to aortic stenosis and its phenotyping is incident aortic stenosis cases, whereas PGS005256 is primarily framed as “Peak aortic velocity” with a broader trait_efo including an aortic measurement component (weaker endpoint fidelity despite also mentioning incident aortic stenosis). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size and design signals; PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005256), suggesting stronger PRS discrimination. Although PGS005252 reports only a full-model C-index (0.87) with heavier clinical covariates (making that metric non-comparable), PGS005256 provides no discrimination metric at all beyond HR, and its larger training N is a weak differentiator. Overall, the combination of tighter disease labeling plus stronger HR favors PGS005252.

PGS001268 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence and evaluation context: it reports explicit PRS-only AUROC (0.7346) and PRS-only R² (0.10232) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and has multi-ancestry evaluation plus a large validation sample (n=67,425). Its PRS-only R² is also plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.399), so it passes the sanity check. PGS003420 is disease-focused and ancestry-matched to EAS, but it lacks PRS-only metrics entirely (only a full-model AUROC=0.7886 with unknown covariates), has no training sample information, and is validated only in a small single-ancestry sample (n=1,298), making its apparent performance less interpretable and less robust for general selection.

PGS001267 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports clean PGS-only AUROC (0.7265) and PGS-only R² (0.0988) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and the PRS-only R² is plausible under the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability ~0.399). It also has substantially larger, clearly described training (UKB; n=269,704) and a much larger validation sample (n=67,425) with multi-ancestry evaluation listed, even though the selected record is EUR. In contrast, PGS003420 provides only a single full-model AUROC (0.7886) with unknown covariates and no PGS-only metrics, making its apparent performance non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven; it also has small validation (n=1,298) and missing training details. While PGS003420 is more disease-focused and EAS-specific, the lack of PRS-only performance and sparse metadata make it less well-supported overall than PGS001267.

PGS004477 is the better match to the target trait "arthritis" on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is the generic parent "arthritis" and phenotyping_reported is "M13 (Other arthritis)", whereas PGS000114 is specifically "Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis" (pediatric-onset subtype) and thus a narrower, age-restricted endpoint mismatch for a generic arthritis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance metrics don’t cleanly differentiate; PGS000114’s AUROC=0.738 is a full-model metric (with sex+PC covariates) and is not comparable as PRS-only evidence. Structurally, PGS004477 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with ~1.06M variants and much larger training/validation in UKB, which is more consistent with capturing polygenic signal for a broad arthritis phenotype than PGS000114’s very sparse 26-variant SparSNP score, despite PGS000114 having a stronger reported OR per SD. Overall, broader phenotype alignment plus stronger polygenic model structure favors PGS004477.

PGS005252 is an exact endpoint match to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo = aortic stenosis; phenotyping_reported = incident aortic stenosis cases), whereas PGS004911 targets a different disease entirely (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) and thus has poor phenotype alignment for aortic stenosis. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.87 vs 0.80) are not decisive and are also less comparable given PGS005252’s heavier clinical covariate set; however, endpoint fidelity dominates and PGS005252 also shows supportive PRS signal via HR=1.92 in a large EUR evaluation (n=446,895). Therefore PGS005252 is better-supported for aortic stenosis than the off-target PGS004911.

PGS004477 is the better match to the target trait "arthritis" on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is arthritis and phenotyping_reported is "M13 (Other arthritis)", whereas PGS001290 is explicitly osteoarthritis (trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), a narrower subtype mismatch for a generic arthritis target. Although PGS001290 provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.52166; R2 0.00109, below the arthritis h2 ceiling) and broader evaluation ancestries, it is a pan-trait sparse UKB framework score ("across 813 traits") with very weak PRS-only performance, while PGS004477 at least comes from a disease-prediction integration study using a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with a moderate OR per SD (~1.20) despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2. Given the tradeoff between stronger phenotype alignment (PGS004477) vs cleaner but weak and subtype-specific framework metrics (PGS001290), PGS004477 narrowly wins, but confidence is low due to its missing comparable PRS-only metrics and unknown covariates.

PGS001135 is the better-supported match to the target trait "arthritis" because its endpoint is explicitly generic arthritis (trait_efo=arthritis; phenotyping_reported="Arthritis (nos)") and it reports clean PRS-only performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.53928; PGS-only R2=0.00291), which are interpretable and below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.061). In contrast, PGS000114 targets a narrower pediatric subtype (juvenile idiopathic arthritis; trait_efo and phenotyping both JIA), which is a meaningful endpoint mismatch for a generic arthritis target, and it lacks PRS-only metrics—only a full-model AUROC (0.738) is shown, which is not comparable as standalone PRS evidence even though it reports an OR. While PGS000114 is disease-focused, the combination of endpoint mismatch and non-comparable performance reporting makes PGS001135 the stronger choice here.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint fidelity is direct: trait_efo is exactly "alcohol dependence" and both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are "Alcohol use disorder" (a close clinical synonym/umbrella for dependence). It also shows stronger PRS signal in the reported effect metrics (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76; β=0.17) than PGS000202 (ΔR²=0.00456; β=0.043), where the reported trait is "Problematic alcohol use" and the mapped EFO is a measurement construct rather than the disease itself. While PGS000202 has cleaner disclosed basic covariates and far more variants, neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R², and PGS002739’s disease-focused AUD-in-African-Americans context plus stronger effect-size evidence outweighs PGS000202’s broader but more proxy-like phenotype framing.

PGS004547 is the better match to the target trait "arthritis" because its endpoint is a broad arthritis diagnosis category (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported: "M13 (Other arthritis)" with trait_efo: arthritis), whereas PGS000114 targets a restricted pediatric subtype (juvenile idiopathic arthritis), which is a meaningful endpoint mismatch for a generic arthritis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance metrics are not cleanly comparable; PGS000114’s AUROC=0.738 is full-model (with covariates) and cannot substitute for PRS-only performance. With metrics largely uninformative, the decision falls back to endpoint fidelity and structural/study signals: PGS004547 has much larger-scale development/validation (UKB; n=174,489 training; n=56,192 validation) and a genome-wide model (1,059,939 variants) consistent with capturing polygenic signal for a broad arthritis phenotype, while PGS000114 is a sparse 26-variant score with small validation (n=940) tailored to JIA. Overall, PGS004547 is more appropriate for the broad arthritis target despite unknown covariates and only moderate OR evidence.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS003973 has a stronger overall evidence package on structural and study-design fields: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.1M variants and is developed in a large multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis context (many contributing cohorts listed), which is generally more robust than the very sparse P+T score in PGS000753 (29 variants) trained on a smaller setting. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS003973’s reported C-index=0.882 is a full-model metric (age/age^2/sex) and cannot be treated as PRS-comparable; however, PGS000753’s only quantitative support is a moderate OR=1.37 per SD and it also uses a prevalent endpoint, which is slightly less clean than the generic AAA endpoint in PGS003973. Given the lack of PRS-only metrics for both, the method/variant-count and multi-cohort disease-focused development advantages favor PGS003973.

PGS002727 is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study with explicit endpoint specificity (phenotyping_reported: Pediatric asthma) and provides supportive PRS signal via a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.57) plus very large, multi-ancestry evaluation breadth (EVAL spans AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS) and large validation N (391,820). PGS001782 comes from a portability/framework-style paper (“Global Biobank analyses…”) and, while it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 covariates-regressed-out = 0.048844, below the asthma heritability ceiling) and uses only basic covariates, it is evaluated only in EUR with a much smaller validation sample (7,128) and lacks effect-size support. Given the framework penalty and weaker validation context for PGS001782, PGS002727 is better-supported overall despite lacking explicit PGS-only AUC/R2.

PGS001135 is the better match to the target trait "arthritis" on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is exactly "arthritis" and phenotyping_reported is "Arthritis (nos)", whereas PGS001290 targets the narrower subtype "osteoarthritis" (trait_efo/phenotyping_reported both osteoarthritis), which is a partial mismatch for a generic arthritis target. Both are otherwise near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical training cohort (UKB), training size, ancestry distribution, and similarly basic covariates, so performance becomes the main differentiator: PGS001135 has higher PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.539 vs 0.522; PGS-only R2 0.00291 vs 0.00109) and a larger variant count (1028 vs 579). Validation N differences are not decisive here. Heritability sanity-check is not violated by either, but PGS001135 shows the stronger PRS signal while also aligning better to the target endpoint.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and have similarly light, non-leaky covariates and identical EUR evaluation size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics essentially tied (HR high vs low PRS 1.249 for PGS002755 vs 1.153 for PGS004587), the structural evidence favors PGS002755: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to polygenic traits like eczema than a 23-SNP genome-wide-significant score (PGS004587). PGS004587’s multi-cohort training list is supportive but not enough to outweigh the much sparser construction and weaker HR signal.

PGS001344 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and endpoint specificity: it targets a clear diagnosis endpoint (“Asthma diagnosed by doctor”) and reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64568; PGS-only R²=0.05973), with basic covariates and values that are plausible under the asthma heritability ceiling. PGS002061 has a similarly aligned asthma endpoint and broader evaluation ancestries, but it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² entirely and provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.1184), which is less directly comparable for PRS discrimination; its larger training set and genome-wide LDpred2 structure don’t outweigh the missing PRS-comparable metrics in this head-to-head.

PGS000114 is more endpoint-faithful to the generic target “arthritis” in a clinically meaningful way: it is a disease-focused PRS for juvenile idiopathic arthritis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all coherent), whereas PGS001290 targets osteoarthritis specifically and comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”), which is explicitly penalized for weaker external generalization. Although PGS001290 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.522; R2 0.00109) and has larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation, those metrics indicate very weak PRS signal and the framework archetype reduces trust; by contrast PGS000114 provides stronger disease-focused evidence including an OR per SD ~2.09 and uses only basic covariates (sex, PCs), but lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 so confidence is not high.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Asthma”) and neither shows problematic clinical-risk packaging; covariates are basic in both. PGS001782 has a directly PRS-comparable metric reported (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2=0.048844), which is interpretable and below the asthma liability h2 ceiling (~0.15), whereas PGS002061 reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.1184) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making cross-model PRS performance comparison weaker. Although PGS002061 has larger training (UKB n=391,124) and broader multi-ancestry evaluation, it comes from a UKB portability framework paper, while PGS001782 is from a global multi-biobank PRS development context; given the cleaner PRS-only R2 evidence plus multi-cohort development, PGS001782 is better supported overall.

PGS002727 is better supported for the target trait asthma because its endpoint is explicitly aligned to a clinically coherent subtype (“Pediatric asthma”) and it provides stronger PRS-relevant evidence via an effect size (OR per SD 1.57, 95% CI 1.55–1.60), whereas PGS005134 reports only an R² value that appears to be full-model/unspecified (no PRS-only metrics and no effect sizes). Although PGS005134 has clean basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a disease-focused multi-cohort meta-analysis context, its evidence package is thin (single record, no training N, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, small validation n=8,741). PGS002727 also shows broader evaluation ancestry coverage and much larger validation support (n=391,820), and its reported full-model AUROC (0.66) is at least consistent with nontrivial signal even if not PRS-only.

PGS004587 is better aligned to the target trait (atopic eczema) at the endpoint level: it targets incident atopic dermatitis in a general prospective cohort context, whereas PGS003459 evaluates a treatment-/context-specific phenotype (“paradoxical eczema in biologic-treated psoriasis”), which is a restricted, therapy-associated subtype and less faithful to generic atopic eczema risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t cleanly differentiate; PGS003459’s AUROC=0.585 is full-model and not PRS-comparable, while PGS004587 at least provides an HR (high vs low PRS) with a very large EUR validation sample (n=337,910) and explicit multi-cohort development (EB/FinnGen/UKB), supporting broader transportability than PGS003459’s small validation (n=3,212) in a niche clinical setting.

PGS004547 is the better-supported choice for the broad target trait “arthritis” because its endpoint is explicitly an arthritis phecode group (“M13 (Other arthritis)”) mapped to EFO:arthritis and it uses a genome-wide/meta-PRS style construction with very large variant coverage (1,059,939) plus a moderate per-SD effect size (OR≈1.26). In contrast, PGS001290 is specifically for osteoarthritis (EFO:osteoarthritis), which is a narrower subtype mismatch for a generic arthritis target, and it comes from a known pan-trait UKB sparse-framework paper (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse model (579 variants) and weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC≈0.522; PGS-only R2≈0.0011). Although PGS001290 reports clean PRS-only metrics and has multi-ancestry evaluation, those metrics are modest and the framework/sparse archetype plus phenotype narrowing make it less compelling than the broader arthritis-aligned, genome-wide score in PGS004547 despite PGS004547 lacking explicit PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS001782 is better supported structurally and by study archetype for asthma: it is a genome-wide shrinkage PRS (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage (884,043) developed across many biobanks (global biobank framework with multi-cohort inputs), and it reports a PRS-comparable metric (covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.048844) with only basic covariates (sex, age, PCs). PGS001344 has slightly higher reported PRS-only metrics in EUR (PGS-only R2=0.05973; PGS-only AUROC=0.64568) and larger validation n, but it comes from the known pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse snpnet framework with a very small SNP set (6,139) and single-biobank development—an archetype that domain guidance flags as less reliable for external generalization. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (doctor-diagnosed vs generic asthma), so the framework/sparsity penalty and broader multi-cohort development tilt the choice to PGS001782 despite the modest metric disadvantage.

PGS002755 has much better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: it is explicitly for incident atopic dermatitis (mapped to atopic eczema), whereas PGS003459 is evaluated on a treatment-induced, restricted phenotype (paradoxical eczema in biologic-treated psoriasis patients) and even broadens the trait to “atopic eczema or atopic disease,” reducing specificity. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS003459’s reported AUROC=0.585 is a full-model metric and not a comparable PRS discriminator; its OR=1.83 is in a niche clinical context. Structurally, PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and is validated in a very large EUR sample (n=337,910), supporting a more generalizable eczema PRS than PGS003459’s 170-SNP GWS score validated in n=3,212.

PGS002755 is better supported for the generic target trait atopic eczema because its phenotyping is an incident atopic dermatitis endpoint in a very large European evaluation sample (n=337,910) and it reports a PRS effect size (HR high vs low PRS=1.249, 95% CI 1.123–1.391) without being tied to a treatment-specific context. In contrast, PGS003486, despite an exact trait label, is explicitly for paradoxical eczema occurring in biologic-treated psoriasis patients (a therapy-induced, restricted subtype endpoint), making it a poorer match to general atopic eczema risk; its only AUROC is a full-model AUROC=0.567 (not PRS-only) from a small sample (n=3,212), so the performance evidence is weaker and less comparable.

PGS004587 has substantially better endpoint fidelity to generic atopic eczema risk: its phenotyping_reported is "Incident atopic dermatitis" in a large prospective cohort context, whereas PGS003486 targets a therapy-specific subtype ("Paradoxical eczema in biologic-treated psoriasis"), which is explicitly a treatment-induced/restricted endpoint and less aligned to the target trait. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS003486’s full-model AUROC=0.567 is not a comparable PRS metric and does not offset the phenotype mismatch. While PGS003486 has more variants (71 vs 23) and an OR=1.89, its restricted endpoint and small validation sample (n=3,212 vs 337,910) make it less reliable for general atopic eczema prediction than PGS004587’s direct incident-disease endpoint with large-scale evaluation (HR high vs low PRS 1.153).

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Asthma”) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/20 PCs), so endpoint fidelity and leakage concerns are essentially tied. PGS001782 has a clearly identified PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2 = 0.048844; Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out), which is directly interpretable as PRS signal and is plausible under the asthma liability h2 ceiling. In contrast, PGS005134 reports only a generic R² (0.053582) presented as “Proportion of the variance explained” and only as full_model_r2 at top level, with no PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out metric, making its performance evidence less cleanly comparable. Validation N is slightly larger for PGS005134 (8,741 vs 7,128) and PRS-CSx is structurally strong, but these are weaker tie-breakers than having an explicit PRS-only R2; therefore PGS001782 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS002755 is the stronger-supported choice for generic atopic eczema risk because its endpoint is a direct disease diagnosis (“Incident atopic dermatitis”) with a very large European evaluation sample (n=337,910) and a genome-wide shrinkage construction (PRS-CS; 1,090,702 variants), which is structurally better suited to a polygenic trait than a 25-variant hit score. PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (“Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis”) and reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.93/0.49) with ethnicity covariates, which is not PRS-comparable and is implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling, suggesting covariate-driven inflation; it also has much smaller validation (n=676). Neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R², so the decision rests on endpoint generality + structural method/variant coverage and evaluation robustness, favoring PGS002755.

PGS002727 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait asthma because it is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study with explicit endpoint framing (phenotyping_reported: Pediatric asthma) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large genome-wide variant coverage (985,837) and broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS split). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only full-model AUROC=0.66 and R²=0.04 are shown), it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.57), which is meaningful PRS signal. In contrast, PGS001344 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6457; PGS-only R²=0.0597, below the asthma h2_liability ceiling) and basic covariates, but it comes from the known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (6,139 variants) that domain guidance flags as less reliable for external transportability; its endpoint is also doctor-diagnosed asthma in UKB rather than a disease-focused asthma-specific development/validation context. Net: PGS002727’s disease-focused design + genome-wide method/coverage outweigh PGS001344’s framework-origin metric cleanliness.

Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method family (genome-wide significant SNPs), have identical evaluation context (EUR-only; n=3,212; covariates PCs 1–2) and the same therapy-specific endpoint (paradoxical eczema in biologic-treated psoriasis), so endpoint fidelity to generic atopic eczema is similarly imperfect for both. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model AUROC is shown and is not a clean PRS-comparable metric. With design essentially tied, PGS003486 has slightly stronger PRS effect-size evidence (OR 1.89 vs 1.83), while PGS003459’s small AUROC edge (0.585 vs 0.567) is a minor full-model difference and not decisive. Hence PGS003486 narrowly wins, but confidence is low due to near-clone records and lack of PRS-only metrics.

PGS005134 is from a disease-focused, multi-cohort asthma meta-analysis study (many biobanks listed in training/development), using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with very large variant coverage (909,298), which is structurally better aligned with a highly polygenic disease like asthma than the sparse UKB pan-trait framework archetype of PGS001344 ("across 813 traits" snpnet, 6,139 variants, UKB-only development). While PGS001344 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.646/0.0597) and multi-ancestry evaluation, it carries the strong framework-paper penalty and its performance advantage is not decisive given the known generalization weakness of these sparse pan-trait UKB scores. PGS005134 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only an R² reported that is likely full-model/ambiguous), which lowers certainty, but overall endpoint fidelity is comparable (both asthma) and the study archetype + method/variant structure favors PGS005134.

PGS002727 is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study (“Multiancestral polygenic risk score for pediatric asthma”) with explicit endpoint specificity (phenotyping_reported: Pediatric asthma) and provides supportive PRS signal via an effect size (OR per SD 1.57) plus reported discrimination (AUROC 0.66, albeit full-model/unspecified PRS-only). It also shows broad multi-ancestry evaluation coverage in the metadata. In contrast, PGS002061 comes from a UKB portability framework paper (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) which domain guidance flags as typically less optimized per-disease; it reports only a modest partial correlation (partial-r 0.1184) and no AUC/R2/effect size, making the PRS strength harder to judge. While PGS002061 has much larger training N and explicit basic covariates, the framework archetype and weaker performance evidence make it less well-supported than the disease-focused PGS002727.

PGS005134 is the better-supported asthma PRS because it comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort asthma meta-analysis (many external biobanks listed in training/development) with clean, basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and reports an R²=0.0536 (though it appears to be a full-model/unspecified R², it is at least a directly asthma-focused performance signal and is below the asthma heritability ceiling). In contrast, PGS002061 is from a UK Biobank portability framework paper (pan-trait/portability archetype), with development in a single cohort (UKB) and its only visible performance is partial-r=0.1184 (not directly comparable to PRS-only R²/AUC), despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation. With both candidates lacking PRS-only AUC/R², the disease-focused multi-cohort design and endpoint-faithful evidence package of PGS005134 outweighs the framework/portability nature of PGS002061.

PGS004587 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait “atopic eczema” because its endpoint is a direct disease incidence phenotype (“Incident atopic dermatitis”) aligned to atopic eczema in EUR evaluation, and it reports a PRS-stratified effect size (HR high vs low PRS = 1.153) in a very large EUR validation sample (n=337,910). In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (“Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis”) and its only strong-looking metrics are full-model AUROC/R² (0.93/0.49) with no PRS-only AUC/R²; given the covariates include parental ethnicity, that discrimination is not directly comparable as PRS performance and the R² is implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling, suggesting it is not PRS-only. Both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores with no PRS-only metrics, so phenotype breadth and metric interpretability favor PGS004587.

PGS001773 has substantially better endpoint fidelity to the target trait (atopic eczema) because its phenotyping/trait are directly moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (a direct eczema subtype), whereas PGS003459 is evaluated on a treatment- and context-specific endpoint ("paradoxical eczema" in biologic-treated psoriasis patients) and even broadens the trait to "atopic eczema or atopic disease," making it less representative of generic atopic eczema risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.93 for PGS001773 vs 0.585 for PGS003459) are not comparable PRS metrics; however, PGS003459 at least provides a PRS effect size (OR 1.83), while PGS001773 provides only covariate-influenced full-model metrics. Despite that, the therapy-induced phenotype mismatch in PGS003459 is a stronger negative signal than the lack of PRS-only metrics in PGS001773, so PGS001773 is better-supported for atopic eczema.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model discrimination metrics are not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS005168’s very high C-index (0.8718) is heavily discounted because covariates include the named clinical risk calculator CHARGE-AF (risk-wrapper packaging), making the reported metric likely covariate-driven rather than PRS-driven. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that packaging concern, and it also shows strong PRS effect size evidence (OR 1.82 per SD) alongside a cross-ancestry PRS-CSx construction with much larger variant coverage (1,271,239 vs 382,963). Despite a smaller validation N (37,161 vs 52,757), the cleaner covariate context and stronger structural/effect-size signals make PGS005313 better-supported for standalone AF PRS use.

PGS001773 is better supported for the target trait (atopic eczema) because its endpoint is a direct atopic dermatitis severity phenotype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis) in a disease-focused Canadian cohort context (CHILD, SLSJ) with demographic covariates, whereas PGS003486’s phenotyping is explicitly treatment/context-specific (“paradoxical eczema in biologic-treated psoriasis”), which is a therapy-induced subtype and a weaker match to generic atopic eczema risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not comparable PRS metrics; however, PGS003486’s full-model AUROC is low (0.567) and its setting suggests outcome heterogeneity, while PGS001773 at least aligns to the core disease entity despite its full-model AUROC likely being covariate-influenced. Overall, endpoint fidelity favors PGS001773 over the more context-restricted PGS003486.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.78 for PGS005313 vs 0.74 for PGS002814) are not decisive PRS-comparable evidence. Given that, structural and transportability signals dominate: PGS005313 uses a genome-wide cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with far broader variant coverage (1,271,239 vs 4,520) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries, whereas PGS002814 is a sparse P+T score evaluated only in East Asians. Effect-size evidence is similar (OR per SD 1.82 for PGS005313 vs ~1.94 for PGS002814), but not enough to outweigh the stronger method/coverage and broader evaluation context of PGS005313.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation). PGS000016 provides a directly PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.029) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, chip), and that R2 is plausible relative to the AF heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.020–0.031). In contrast, PGS005168 reports only a covariate-inflated full-model C-index/AUC (0.8718) while explicitly including a named clinical risk calculator (CHARGE-AF) in covariates, which is strong packaging/leakage evidence and makes its discrimination non-comparable to standalone PRS performance despite its disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS context and strong HR per SD (1.67). Given the need for clean PRS evidence over risk-wrapper performance, PGS000016 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target trait (atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index values are not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS005168 is from a disease-focused AF meta-analysis but its reported performance is explicitly packaged with the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator in the covariates, making the high full-model C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and weak evidence about standalone PRS quality. PGS000331 uses only basic demographic/PC/batch covariates (age, sex, cohort, array/batch, PCs) with an incident AF endpoint, avoiding clinical risk-calculator packaging; it also shows a strong HR per SD (1.62) under a cleaner model context. Given the strong negative signal for risk-calculator covariate packaging in PGS005168 and the cleaner comparability of PGS000331, PGS000331 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the target trait atrial flutter because it has exact endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R²=0.025), which is interpretable and below the heritability ceiling noted in the context. In contrast, PGS002050 uses a broader combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”) rather than flutter-specific, and it lacks PRS-only AUC/R² (only partial correlation is provided), making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for this head-to-head despite its larger variant count and training N.

PGS002814 is from a disease-focused, multi-cohort AF GWAS/meta-analysis context (AFGen, BBJ, FinnGen, HUNT, MGI, MyCode, UKB, deCODE) with basic covariates only (age/sex/PCs) and reports strong PRS effect size evidence (OR≈1.94 per SD; β=0.66), supporting meaningful standalone PRS signal even though only full-model AUROC/R2 are shown. PGS000016 provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.029, below the AF h2_obs ceiling) and has broader multi-ancestry evaluation, but it is a single-biobank (UKB) framework-style score with modest PRS-only R2 and its headline AUROC is also full-model. Given endpoint parity (both AF) and the domain guidance favoring disease-focused multi-cohort models when metric evidence is not clearly superior, PGS002814 is better supported overall.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable as PRS performance. However, PGS005168’s reported performance is explicitly tied to a covariate package that includes the named clinical risk calculator CHARGE-AF (age/sex plus clinical predictors), which is strong risk-wrapper/clinical packaging and makes its high full-model C-index (0.8718) largely non-informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that packaging concern, and still shows strong per-SD effect size evidence (OR≈1.94) consistent with meaningful PRS signal. Given cleaner covariate comparability and strong effect size support, PGS002814 is better-supported despite smaller variant count and lower full-model AUROC.

PGS000016 is better supported for standalone AF PRS selection because it reports a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.029) with basic covariates and this R2 is plausible under the AF heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.020–0.031), whereas PGS000331 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model C-index (0.751) plus HR=1.62 that are less directly comparable to PRS performance. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (AF vs incident AF), but PGS000331’s incident time-to-event framing and reliance on full-model discrimination make its evidence package less clean than PGS000016’s explicit PRS-only R2; other differences (training/validation size, cohorts, ancestry) do not clearly outweigh that metric advantage.

PGS001263 is a direct endpoint match to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”), whereas PGS001841 uses a combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is less specific to atrial flutter alone. PGS001263 also reports clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R²=0.025), and the R² is plausible under the provided heritability ceiling guidance (well below liability h²). By contrast, PGS001841 provides only partial correlation (partial-r=0.1026) and no PRS-only AUROC/R², making its predictive evidence less directly comparable despite larger training N and slightly broader evaluation ancestries. Both are UKB framework-style scores, so the deciding advantages are endpoint fidelity and availability of PRS-only performance metrics, favoring PGS001263.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all basal cell carcinoma), same publication/study family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sample sizes, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not decisive). With performance essentially indistinguishable (full-model AUROC 0.632 vs 0.630; pseudo-R² 0.0487 vs 0.0456), the tiny AUROC/R² edge favors PGS000452, while PGS000456’s slightly higher top-1% OR is not enough to outweigh the overall near-tie.

PGS005313 is better supported for the target trait (atrial fibrillation) because it has cleaner endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported is simply “atrial fibrillation” vs PGS000331’s “Incident atrial fibrillation,” which is a narrower time-to-event framing) and stronger PRS signal evidence via effect size (OR per SD 1.82 vs HR 1.62). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so neither can be promoted on comparable PRS-only discrimination; their reported AUROC/C-index values are full-model and not directly comparable, especially given different covariate sets. PGS005313 also has broader multi-ancestry GWAS input and multi-ancestry evaluation context (vs PGS000331 largely EUR-focused), supporting transportability. Overall, PGS005313 has the stronger disease-focused, cross-population evidence package, while PGS000331’s main advantages (more variants, multiple records) don’t outweigh the weaker endpoint specificity and smaller effect size.

PGS002814 is better supported for the target trait (atrial fibrillation) because it comes from a clearly disease-focused, cross-ancestry AF GWAS/meta-analysis context with very large multi-cohort development (n=1,150,799; AFGen/BBJ/FinnGen/UKB/deCODE etc.) and reports strong PRS effect size evidence (OR per SD ~1.94). Although it only provides full-model metrics (AUROC 0.74 with basic covariates age/sex/PCs) and no PGS-only AUC/R2, PGS000331 also lacks PGS-only metrics and its reported discrimination is likewise full-model (C-index 0.751) in an incident time-to-event setting. With comparable metric limitations, PGS002814’s stronger disease-specific study archetype and larger, more externally oriented multi-biobank training support outweigh PGS000331’s methodological advantage (LDpred, genome-wide variants) and slightly higher full-model C-index, which is not PRS-comparable.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity for the target (both report/phenotype “Atrial fibrillation and flutter” with the same EFO mapping), come from the same UKB portability paper, use the same training cohort (UKB; n=391,124), have identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), identical validation size (n=19,230) and identical multi-ancestry evaluation distribution. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are structural: PGS002050 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (554,908) versus PGS001841’s sparse penalized regression score with 3,980 variants. The observed partial-r is also marginally higher for PGS002050 (0.1034 vs 0.1026), consistent with (though not decisive over) the structural advantage. Given the same framework context and essentially identical phenotype/covariate setup, PGS002050 is better-supported.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and only basic covariates (PGS005313: age, sex; PGS000016: age, sex, PCs, chip). However, PGS005313 is supported by a disease-focused, multi-cohort cross-population AF study (AFGen, BBJ, FinnGen, MVP, UKB, deCODE, etc.) with explicitly multi-ancestry GWAS input and multi-ancestry evaluation, and it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.82), which is strong evidence of PRS discrimination even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided. PGS000016 provides a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.029), which is below the AF heritability ceiling and informative, but it comes from a single-biobank (UKB) development context and lacks effect-size support here; its full-model AUROC (0.77) is not a substitute for PRS-only performance. Overall, the broader disease-focused multi-cohort/ancestry support plus strong OR makes PGS005313 better-supported despite missing PRS-only R2.

PGS001263 is the better match to the target trait (atrial flutter) with direct endpoint labeling across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS001339 uses a combined atrial fibrillation+flutter time-to-event phenotype (less endpoint-fidel for a pure flutter target and explicitly TTE). Both are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with identical training size, covariates, and validation N, and both report clean PRS-only metrics well below the heritability ceiling; however PGS001263 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC (0.617 vs 0.613) and PRS-only R2 (0.02517 vs 0.02447) while avoiding the AF+flutter composite/TTE packaging.
