Given otherwise identical endpoint fidelity and study context, PGS000639 is better supported by consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62), aligning with the guidance to use effect sizes/structural signals when PRS-only metrics are absent. Method/structure also mildly favors PGS000639 (P+T with 20 variants vs GWAS hits with 16) within the same study family.

Both candidates are near-clones for Hodgkin’s lymphoma: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Hodgkin’s disease), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training n=736, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation n=775. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot compare clean PRS-only discrimination. Given this, the only differentiator is the very small edge in the reported (full-model) metrics/effect sizes: PGS000637 has slightly higher AUROC (0.574 vs 0.569) and slightly higher Nagelkerke R² (0.013 vs 0.0109) with essentially identical OR per SD. The differences are tiny and likely noise, hence low confidence, but PGS000637 is marginally better-supported than PGS000640 on the visible performance fields.

PGS002763 is the better-supported match to the target trait hip osteoarthritis because its endpoint is directly aligned across fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate hip osteoarthritis), whereas PGS002750 targets a treatment/proxy endpoint (total hip replacement / hip replacement) which is a more downstream, severity- and practice-influenced phenotype. With no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported for either candidate, the effect-size evidence and structural properties matter more: PGS002763 shows a stronger per-SD OR (1.38 vs 1.23) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS with ~1,052,273 variants) versus a sparse 37-SNP genome-wide-significant score in PGS002750, which is less likely to capture polygenic signal for OA. Although PGS002763 includes a larger validation sample (39,444 vs 1,257), that is secondary; the decisive advantages are endpoint fidelity and stronger PRS signal/structure.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity and study context (same publication, trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma; same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same cohorts, same covariates, same training n=736 and validation n=775) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak differentiator. Given that, PGS000638 has consistently stronger reported validation performance than PGS000637 on the available comparable fields: higher full-model AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke pseudo-R² (0.0193 vs 0.013), with slightly higher per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). The much larger variant count in PGS000637 (PRS-CS) does not outweigh the observed weaker performance within this same-endpoint sibling pair.

PGS002763 is the better-supported match to the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is direct: phenotyping_reported is "Hip osteoarthritis" (aligned with target), whereas PGS002728 uses "Total hip replacement," a treatment/proxy endpoint that can reflect access/surgical decision and disease severity rather than hip OA status. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002728’s reported AUROC=0.66 is a full-model metric (age/sex-adjusted) and not a clean PRS-comparable advantage. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants and reports a moderate per-SD OR=1.38, supporting genuine polygenic signal capture; PGS002728 is a 44-variant genome-wide-significant score, which is more likely to miss polygenic architecture for hip OA. Both are EUR-only evaluation; PGS002728’s multi-cohort development is supportive but does not outweigh the endpoint mismatch and weaker structural PRS properties.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication, use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and have identical EUR-only training/evaluation context and sample sizes (training n=736; validation n=775), so endpoint fidelity and transportability do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on the available full-model metrics and effect sizes as supportive evidence. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger performance signals than PGS000640: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.569), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0276 vs 0.0109), and stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.476 vs 1.292). Given otherwise near-identical design, these empirical differences favor PGS000639 over the lassosum sibling despite PGS000640’s much larger variant count.

Both candidates are from the same Nat Commun study, target the same endpoint (trait_efo/trait_reported hypertension; phenotyping_reported prevalent hypertension), use the same covariates, have the same training N (10,314) and validation N (39,035), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only near-identical full-model AUROC ~0.764 vs 0.763, which is not a strong differentiator). PGS004236 is better-supported because it provides additional PRS-relevant evidence (effect size OR=2.1 with CI) that PGS004234 lacks, and it is developed on a broader set of cohorts (BioMe+MVP+UKB vs BioMe+UKB), consistent with a more robust multi-cohort construction. Variant count is also higher for PGS004236 (398,805 vs 234,228), a mild structural advantage in the absence of PRS-only metrics.

PGS000638 has coherent endpoint fidelity to Hodgkin’s lymphoma across fields (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both “Hodgkin’s disease”, trait_efo matches), whereas PGS003449 is internally inconsistent for the target because phenotyping_reported is “Chronic lymphocytic leukemia” despite trait_reported/EFO saying Hodgkin lymphoma—this is a major phenotype mismatch/contamination signal. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t rescue PGS003449; PGS000638 at least reports a basic-covariate full-model AUROC (0.601 with age/sex/PCs/batch) and a moderate per-SD OR (1.377), while PGS003449 shows a near-null OR (1.02). Ancestry is EUR-only for both; the larger validation N in PGS003449 cannot outweigh its explicit endpoint mismatch.

PGS000640 is endpoint-faithful to the target (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma) with basic, non-leaky covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs) and shows at least moderate PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.292, CI 1.011–1.651) plus a reported AUROC (0.569) albeit full-model. In contrast, PGS003449 has a critical phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is “Chronic lymphocytic leukemia,” which is not Hodgkin lymphoma, making its performance/effect size (OR 1.02, 0.97–1.08) non-informative for the target and suggesting very weak PRS signal anyway. Despite PGS003449’s larger validation sample size, the endpoint incoherence dominates, so PGS000640 is better supported for Hodgkin lymphoma.

PGS000639 is endpoint-faithful to Hodgkin’s lymphoma across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (all Hodgkin’s disease) and provides coherent evaluation details (EUR-only, basic covariates age/sex/PCs) plus supportive effect size (OR per SD 1.476) and a reported AUROC (0.62, albeit full-model). In contrast, PGS003449 has a major endpoint mismatch: phenotyping_reported is "Chronic lymphocytic leukemia" despite trait_efo being Hodgkins lymphoma, and its only effect size is near-null (OR 1.02). Even with larger validation N, the phenotype incoherence and weak signal make PGS003449 less supported for Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Both candidates match the target trait (hypertension) at the trait_reported/trait_efo level, but PGS004236 is from a disease-focused multi-ethnic hypertension study with multi-cohort development (BioMe, MVP, UKB) and explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation, plus a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1). In contrast, PGS001320 comes from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework, which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization despite having clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649). PGS004236’s reported AUROC (0.764) is full-model and covariate-influenced (age/sex/BMI/smoking etc.) so it can’t be used as PRS-only evidence, but the combination of disease-focused design, multi-cohort context, and strong OR support outweighs the framework-score advantage of PGS001320’s PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo = Hodgkins lymphoma), study context (same Cancer PRSweb paper), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), training size (n=736) and validation size (n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not directly comparable PRS metrics). With those major fields tied, the best differentiator is the within-family empirical performance: PGS000638 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.601 vs 0.569) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.0109), plus slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.377 vs 1.292). Although PGS000640 uses a genome-wide lassosum model with many variants, its observed discrimination/effect-size evidence is weaker here, so PGS000638 is better-supported on the visible record.

Both candidates match the target trait (hypertension) well, but PGS004236 has stronger disease-focused, multi-cohort and multi-ancestry support: it is explicitly a multi-ethnic hypertension PRS developed using multiple cohorts (BioMe, MVP, UKB) and evaluated across several ancestries, and it reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1). In contrast, PGS002335 comes from a portability/methods-focused paper, is trained in EUR-only UKB with training sample size not reported, and its only reported metric is an incremental R2=0.0527 (not a clean PRS-only R2), offering weaker direct evidence of standalone PRS signal. PGS004236’s reported AUROC is full-model and covariate-influenced (so not PRS-comparable), but overall its endpoint fidelity plus multi-cohort/multi-ancestry design and strong OR make it better supported than PGS002335.

Both candidates are near-clones for the hyperthyroidism target: same endpoint fidelity (Graves’ disease; phenotyping_reported graves’ disease), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC reported, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With design/metadata essentially tied, PGS005265 has slightly stronger visible performance/effect evidence (full-model AUROC 0.6652 vs 0.6637; OR per SD 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434) and a trivially higher variant count, so it edges PGS005266, but the differences are small hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (hypertension), same publication and release date, same training cohort (UKB), same covariates (basic demographics/PCs), identical ancestry distribution (EUR GWAS; 4-way eval) and identical validation sample size (n=43,392). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; both only provide incremental/full-model R2, which is not a clean standalone PRS metric. With endpoints and evaluation context effectively tied, the only differentiator is the reported incremental R2, where PGS002652 is marginally higher (0.0539 vs 0.0527 for PGS002335); this small gap is likely noise, hence low confidence, but it is the only visible advantage.

PGS004234 is from a hypertension-focused, explicitly multi-ethnic study with multi-ancestry development/validation context (BioMe+UKB; DEV includes AFR/AMR/EUR/ASN; EVAL MAE), which is stronger transportability evidence for the generic target trait than PGS001320’s pan-trait UKB framework origin ("across 813 traits") that is specifically flagged as underperforming in external cohorts. While PGS001320 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.629; PGS-only R2 0.0649) and PGS004234 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a covariate-influenced full-model AUROC 0.763 with BMI/smoking etc.), the framework penalty plus weaker external-cohort orientation makes PGS001320 less well-supported overall for real-world hypertension PRS selection. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both, but PGS004234’s disease-focused multi-ancestry validation outweighs PGS001320’s metric completeness here.

PGS004236 is better supported for the target trait hypertension because it comes from a hypertension-focused multi-ethnic study with explicit disease-relevant evidence (OR=2.1 with tight CI) and multi-cohort development/validation (BioMe, MVP, UKB; validation n=39,035 across multiple ancestries). Although its only AUROC shown is a full-model AUROC=0.764 (not PRS-only) and includes additional epidemiologic covariates (e.g., BMI, smoking), it still provides stronger direct PRS signal via effect size than PGS002652. PGS002652 is from a portability/methods paper context and reports only an incremental/full-model R2=0.0539 (not a clean PRS-only metric), with training sample size listed as N/A and UKB-only development; despite a slightly larger validation n=43,392 and cleaner basic covariates, it lacks comparable PRS-only performance and effect-size evidence. Overall, endpoint alignment is similar, but PGS004236 has the more disease-focused evidence package and stronger PRS signal reporting.

Both candidates match the target phenotype cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Hypertension”) and use only basic demographic/PC-style covariates, so endpoint fidelity and leakage concerns are similar. PGS001320 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.0649 (and incremental AUROC), enabling direct PRS assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check, whereas PGS002652 provides only an incremental/full-model R² (0.0539) with no PRS-only AUC/R² and no training sample size, leaving its standalone PRS signal less evidenced in the visible fields. Although PGS002652 has a method/structure advantage (PolyFun-pred; many more variants), the lack of comparable PRS-only metrics makes it less well-supported here than PGS001320’s clearer PRS-only validation evidence.

Both candidates match the target phenotype cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Hypertension”) and use only basic demographic/PC-style covariates, so endpoint fidelity and leakage risk are similar. PGS001320 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.0649 (and incremental AUROC), which are interpretable as standalone PRS metrics and are below the hypertension heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.36), making them plausible. PGS002335, despite a stronger structural profile (genome-wide BOLT-LMM with ~1.1M variants and a disease-focused Nat Genet context), lacks PRS-only AUC/R² and provides only an incremental R² (0.0527) without standalone PRS discrimination, leaving weaker directly comparable evidence on this record. Given the similar phenotype/covariate setup, the presence of clean PRS-only metrics makes PGS001320 the more evidence-supported choice here.

Both candidates match the target trait (hypertension) at the trait_reported/trait_efo level, but PGS002335 has cleaner endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported="Hypertension") whereas PGS004234 is explicitly "Prevelant hypertension" (a narrower prevalence-defined endpoint). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004234’s full-model AUROC=0.763 is not a comparable PRS metric and is further confounded by a heavier covariate set including BMI and smoking. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural/transportability signals matter more: PGS002335 uses a genome-wide model (BOLT-LMM) with substantially broader variant coverage (1,109,311 vs 234,228) and has explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), while PGS004234’s evaluation is MAE-only. Validation sample sizes are similar, so they don’t break the tie. Overall, PGS002335 is better-supported as a standalone hypertension PRS on the visible fields.

PGS005265 is better supported for a generic hyperthyroidism target because its endpoint is Graves’ disease (the clinically dominant autoimmune form of hyperthyroidism) and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank study with broad external evaluation (multiple contributing cohorts; EVAL MAE 100%; validation n=94,651). It also reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD ~1.63), which is meaningful PRS signal even though only a full-model AUROC is shown (0.665) and covariates are unknown. In contrast, PGS001042 is an exact-label thyrotoxicosis/hyperthyroidism time-to-event phenotype, but it is from the known pan-trait UKB sparse framework (“across 813 traits”), with a very sparse 226-variant snpnet model and only modest PRS-only performance (PGS AUROC 0.634; PGS R2 0.0236). Given the framework penalty and weaker structural properties, PGS005265’s disease-focused, dominant-subtype alignment and stronger effect-size evidence outweigh PGS001042’s cleaner PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates target Graves’ disease (a strong match to the broader target hyperthyroidism) with identical phenotyping_reported, same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix, and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). Given this near-clone context, structural and effect-size evidence dominate: PGS005266 (PRSCS; 1,085,170 variants) shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR=1.54, β=0.434) than PGS005264 (P+T; 112 variants; OR≈1.01, β=0.008), indicating materially stronger PRS signal. The tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.664 vs 0.659) is negligible, so PGS005266 is better-supported overall.

PGS004234 is better supported for the target trait hypertension because it comes from a hypertension-focused multi-ethnic study with explicit multi-ancestry development/validation context (DEV includes AFR/AMR/EUR/ASN; EVAL is MAE) and a large external validation sample (n=39,035). Although its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.763 (not PRS-only) and includes additional epidemiologic covariates (smoking, BMI), it is still endpoint-faithful (prevalent hypertension) and not a portability/framework sweep. In contrast, PGS002652 is from a methods/portability-style paper (fine-mapping/multipopulation training) with UKB-only development, no training N reported, and only an incremental R2=0.0539 tied to a combined model (“when combined with BOLT-LMM vs covariates alone”), which is less directly interpretable as standalone PRS performance; its selected validation ancestry is European despite multi-ancestry evaluation listed. With both lacking clean PRS-only AUC/R2, the stronger disease-focused, explicitly multi-ethnic validation context of PGS004234 is the deciding advantage.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet paper with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported both hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), identical covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same development cohorts, and same validation sample size (n=343,182). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family discriminator. Within this otherwise matched setting, PGS004911 has consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5) and is additionally labeled as an MTAG-enhanced version, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base variant when endpoints are the same.

PGS005265 is better supported for the target trait (hyperthyroidism) because its endpoint is Graves’ disease, which is a clinically dominant autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation context (multiple cohorts; EVAL MAE 100% with validation n=94,651). It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.63), which is meaningful PRS evidence even though only a full-model AUROC is shown (and PRS-only AUC/R2 are missing). In contrast, PGS001043 matches the umbrella label exactly and provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC=0.6323; PGS R2=0.0216, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants, UKB-only development), which is a systematic generalization risk versus a disease-focused multi-cohort score. Net: the disease-focused, Graves-aligned model (PGS005265) edges out the framework sparse UKB score (PGS001043) despite weaker directly comparable PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), but PGS004911 is structurally a stronger standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with 374,114 variants versus PGS000739’s 27 genome-wide significant hits, which is generally better for polygenic signal capture. The reported AUROCs (0.80 vs 0.821) are full-model and not PRS-only for either, so they are not a clean differentiator; moreover PGS000739’s metric is paired with heavier clinical covariates (multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its full-model AUROC less comparable to PRS performance than PGS004911’s basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). PGS004911 also reports PRS-linked effect sizes (OR per SD 1.33; HR 2.34; OR high vs median tertile 5.9), providing additional PRS-relevant evidence that PGS000739 lacks in the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with identical training size (n=269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and the same DEV/EVAL ancestry distribution; both report clean PRS-only metrics and similar validation size (n=67,425). Candidate_b (PGS001042) has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.63392/0.02359 vs 0.6323/0.02158) and more variants (226 vs 69), but it is explicitly a time-to-event endpoint ("TTE thyrotoxicosis"), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity negative for a generic hyperthyroidism target. Candidate_a (PGS001043) is a more direct disease-status phenotype ("Hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis") matching the target trait more straightforwardly. Given the tiny metric differences and the endpoint-type penalty for candidate_b, PGS001043 is marginally better supported.

PGS004910 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity matches the generic disease concept (phenotyping_reported: “Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy”), whereas PGS000778’s phenotyping is restricted to “clinical events in individuals with a pathogenic or likely pathogenic sarcomeric variant,” a narrower, variant-carrier subgroup that is less aligned to general-population HCM risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator; however PGS004910 at least provides a large EUR evaluation (n=343,182) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and additional effect-size evidence (e.g., HR 1.97, OR high vs median tertile 5.5), while PGS000778 has sparse construction (20 genome-wide significant variants), unclear evaluation ancestry (“Not reported”), and weaker effect size (HR 1.28).

PGS005266 is better supported for the target trait (hyperthyroidism) because its endpoint is Graves’ disease, which is explicitly the dominant autoimmune form of clinical hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused multi-biobank study with broad external cohort context (AllofUs, FinnGen, MVP, UKB, etc.) and multi-ancestry evaluation. Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC=0.664 plus effect sizes, including OR per SD ≈1.54), the study archetype and endpoint fidelity are strong. In contrast, PGS001043 matches the umbrella label exactly and reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC=0.632, PGS R2=0.0216, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse snpnet framework with very few variants (69) and single-biobank development, which is a systematic generalization risk relative to a disease-focused multi-cohort score. Net: the disease-focused, Graves-as-hyperthyroidism model (PGS005266) is the more reliable choice despite weaker directly comparable metrics.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are hypothyroidism) and use the same method family (PRS-CS) with similar genome-wide variant counts (~1.09–1.11M) and EUR evaluation. However, PGS005218’s only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.859 while explicitly adjusting for near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making that AUROC largely non-comparable to standalone PRS performance and potentially covariate-driven. In contrast, PGS002766 reports a PRS effect size (OR per SD=1.47, 95% CI 1.43–1.52) under basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), which is more directly interpretable as genetic signal for hypothyroidism risk. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the cleaner covariate context and PRS-specific effect size evidence make PGS002766 better-supported overall despite its smaller validation sample and sparser metadata.

PGS005218 is better supported overall: it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with much broader multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), far larger training (n=1,146,562) and evaluation (n=441,692), and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,110,091), which is structurally favorable for a polygenic disease. Although its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC (0.859) that is likely inflated by explicit thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) and thus not PRS-comparable, candidate_b (PGS004935) is a portability/framework-style single-UKB SnpNet score with sparse variants (6,127), much smaller evaluation (n=8,417), and only a modest full-model AUROC (0.7); its OR=1.5 is supportive but does not outweigh the stronger endpoint-specific, multi-cohort evidence package of PGS005218.

Both candidates match the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo = hypothyroidism) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. PGS005218’s reported AUROC=0.859 is heavily discounted because its covariates explicitly include near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making the full-model discrimination largely non-PRS-driven and non-comparable. PGS005269, while having a lower full-model AUROC (0.639) and unknown covariates, avoids explicit biomarker leakage and provides supportive PRS signal via effect sizes (OR per SD ≈1.65), plus evaluation across multiple ancestries (AA/HL/EUR) rather than EUR-only. Net: PGS005269 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for hypothyroidism given less explicit clinical-covariate inflation and stronger PRS-specific effect-size evidence.

PGS005264 is better supported for the target trait (hyperthyroidism) because its endpoint is Graves’ disease, which is a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused global multi-biobank study with broad external validation ancestry (African American/Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, European) and a large validation sample (n=94,651). PGS001043 matches the target label more literally (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and reports clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.6323; R²=0.02158, below the stated heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) which is explicitly cautioned to generalize less well; its evaluation is also primarily European in the selected record. Because PGS005264 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² (only a full-model AUROC=0.6587 with unknown covariates and very weak per-SD OR≈1.008), the win is driven mainly by endpoint plausibility plus disease-focused multi-cohort/transportability context rather than stronger comparable performance, hence low confidence.

PGS005266 is better supported for the target trait hyperthyroidism because its endpoint is Graves’ disease (a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism) with direct diagnosis phenotyping (“graves’ disease”), and it comes from a disease-focused multi-biobank study with large external-style validation (n=94,651) and multi-ancestry evaluation context. Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a full-model AUROC=0.664 plus a strong per-SD OR≈1.54), the study archetype and endpoint fidelity align well with the target. In contrast, PGS001042 is an exact-label thyrotoxicosis/hyperthyroidism time-to-event phenotype from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet, 226 variants); despite clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.634, R²=0.0236, below the heritability ceiling), the framework origin and TTE packaging are negative signals for external reliability versus a disease-focused Graves’ score.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a reliable differentiator—especially since PGS000739’s AUROC=0.821 is paired with heavy clinical covariates (multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its discrimination likely covariate-driven and less comparable to a standalone PRS. PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that leakage concern, and is a genome-wide shrinkage score (PRS-CS) with very large variant count (374,190 vs 27), which is structurally more appropriate for polygenic signal capture when PRS-only metrics are absent. Validation is also larger for PGS004910 (n=343,182 vs n=184,511), providing mild additional support. Overall, PGS004910 is better-supported as a cleaner PRS for HCM, while PGS000739’s apparent performance advantage is not PRS-comparable due to covariate packaging.

PGS000739 has much better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is direct “Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy,” whereas PGS000778 targets “Clinical events in individuals with a pathogenic or likely pathogenic sarcomeric variant,” a restricted, genetically ascertained subgroup/outcome package rather than general HCM disease risk. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t cleanly differentiate; PGS000739’s only AUROC is full-model (0.821) and covariate-inflated, but PGS000778 provides only modest effect sizes (HR 1.28) on a very small validation (n=368) with evaluation ancestry not reported. PGS000739 also has clearer transportability context and substantially larger training/validation scale (training n=47,737; validation n=184,511; EUR/MAE evaluation) than PGS000778, making it the better-supported HCM PRS overall despite covariate-heavy modeling.

PGS005264 is better supported for the target trait hyperthyroidism because its endpoint is a clinically dominant subtype match (Graves’ disease) and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation context (multiple cohorts listed; eval ancestry MAE 100% with validation n=94,651). In contrast, PGS001042 is an older UK Biobank pan-trait framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event thyrotoxicosis endpoint and, despite having clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6339; PGS R2 0.0236, below the heritability ceiling), it is exactly the kind of sparse single-biobank framework model that domain guidance warns tends to generalize worse than disease-focused multi-cohort alternatives. PGS005264 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC 0.6587 and tiny per-unit effect sizes), which lowers confidence, but the stronger study archetype and acceptable phenotype fidelity (Graves as dominant hyperthyroidism form) outweigh PGS001042’s metric completeness.

Both candidates target Graves’ disease (a strong clinical match to the broader target hyperthyroidism), come from the same publication, have identical ancestry distribution, cohorts, and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With endpoint and study context essentially tied, PGS005265 is better supported by stronger structural and empirical signals: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with far more variants (1,085,173 vs 112) and shows materially stronger effect size evidence (OR per SD 1.63 vs 1.01; β 0.486 vs 0.008). The small full-model AUROC difference (0.665 vs 0.659) is minor, but it is directionally consistent with PGS005265 being the stronger score.

PGS004911 is better supported for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because its endpoint fidelity is direct (phenotyping_reported: “Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy”) and it comes from a disease-focused evaluation study with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a very large EUR validation sample (n=343,182). Although its reported AUROC=0.8 and R²=0.048 are full-model (not PRS-only), it at least provides a coherent performance package plus strong effect-size separation (e.g., OR high vs median tertile 5.9; HR 2.34). In contrast, PGS000778 has weaker endpoint alignment (phenotyping_reported is “Clinical events in individuals with a pathogenic or likely pathogenic sarcomeric variant,” i.e., a restricted genetically ascertained subgroup rather than general HCM), much sparser construction (20 variants), non-comparable/unclear ancestry context (GWAS: MAE; EVAL: not reported), and only modest effect-size evidence (HR 1.28). With neither candidate providing PRS-only AUC/R², the stronger phenotype match and disease-focused general-population evaluation context favor PGS004911.

Both candidates match the target trait (hypothyroidism) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. PGS005218’s very high full-model AUROC (0.859) is heavily confounded by explicit near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) in the covariates, making its performance largely non-informative for standalone PRS quality despite large EUR-only training/validation. PGS005268 has less covariate-leakage risk on the visible fields (covariates unknown rather than explicitly biomarker-heavy) and provides PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD ≈1.66), plus evaluation across multiple ancestries (MAE; selected validation ancestry includes African American/Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, European), supporting broader transportability. Given the severe biomarker adjustment in PGS005218 and the presence of PRS effect-size evidence and multi-ancestry evaluation for PGS005268, PGS005268 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are EUR-only in development/evaluation, with similar per-SD ORs (PGS004935 OR=1.5 vs PGS002766 OR=1.47). However, PGS004935’s only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.70 with covariates listed as Unknown, which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven; it provides limited clean evidence about standalone PRS performance. PGS002766, while also lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, at least documents a standard basic covariate set (age, sex, PCs, technical covariates) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (1,092,122 vs 6,127), a structural advantage for a polygenic disease when other evidence is similar. Validation N is larger for PGS002766 (39,444 vs 8,417) but treated only as minor support. Overall, PGS002766 is better-supported on methodological/structural grounds and has cleaner disclosed modeling context than PGS004935’s non-comparable full-model AUROC with unknown covariates.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC in PGS005269 (0.639) is not a comparable PRS metric. PGS002766 has cleaner, explicitly stated basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical) and a well-defined EUR GWAS/EUR evaluation context, whereas PGS005269 has unknown covariates and an unclear GWAS ancestry label (NR) despite multi-cohort training. Effect-size evidence is similar but slightly favors PGS005269 (OR 1.65 vs 1.47), yet given the covariate uncertainty and non-comparable AUROC, PGS002766 is better-supported on the visible metadata.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait/phenotyping (hypothyroidism), same EFO, same method (PRSCS), essentially identical variant counts (~1.085M), same evaluation ancestry and validation N (94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC reported, with unknown covariates). With endpoints and evidence packages effectively identical, the only differentiators are tiny performance/effect-size differences and cohort list breadth. PGS005268 has marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.6389 vs 0.6386) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.658 vs 1.652) and includes additional development cohorts (BBJ, CKB) not listed for PGS005269, so it is very slightly better supported; however the differences are minimal, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (PGS004935 0.70 vs PGS005269 0.639) are not clean PRS-comparable differentiators. PGS005269 is better supported overall by a stronger external/transportability evidence package: it is developed across many biobanks (AllofUs, MVP, FinnGen, UKB, etc.) and validated at much larger scale (n=94,651) with multi-ancestry evaluation (includes African American/LatAm/European), whereas PGS004935 is essentially UKB-only development with small EUR-only validation (n=8,417) and comes from a portability-style paper. Effect-size evidence is also at least as strong for PGS005269 (OR~1.65) as PGS004935 (OR~1.5).

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC in PGS005268 (0.639) cannot be treated as a clean PRS discriminator. The main differentiators are study/transportability evidence and effect size: PGS005268 comes from a large disease-focused multi-biobank, multi-ancestry development set (AllofUs, MVP, FinnGen, UKB, etc.) with a larger validation sample (n=94,651) and a stronger per-SD OR (1.66) than PGS002766 (OR 1.47) from a cross-disease family-history comparison paper with EUR-only evaluation (n=39,444). Covariates are unknown for PGS005268 (reduces confidence), but PGS002766’s cleaner covariate listing does not outweigh the broader external/ancestry context and stronger effect-size evidence supporting PGS005268.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training size, and identical ancestry distribution/validation size; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, only partial-r. With metrics essentially tied (partial-r 0.1355 for PGS002031 vs 0.1307 for PGS001823, overlapping CIs), the main differentiator is structural: PGS002031 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with substantially more variants (6713 vs 654), which is generally favored for polygenic signal capture when other fields are equal. Therefore PGS002031 is better supported, though confidence is only moderate given the small performance gap and shared framework origin.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint fidelity is an exact match at all visible fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different trait_efo and phenotyping_reported. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.738 vs 0.76) is not a reliable differentiator; instead, PGS000114 has stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51) and a larger variant set (26 vs 12) within the same method (SparSNP) and same basic covariates/ancestry context. Validation size favors PGS000326, but this is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the exact endpoint match plus stronger OR for PGS000114.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all the broad JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a generic JIA target). Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC). Given that full-model AUROC differences (0.738 vs 0.80) are not decisive without PRS-only metrics and the subtype mismatch is the primary fidelity signal, the broad JIA score (PGS000114) is preferred despite PGS000325 having a larger validation sample and higher full-model AUROC.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate hypothyroidism) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.70 for PGS004935 vs 0.639 for PGS005268) are not decisive or directly comparable as PRS metrics. PGS005268 is better supported structurally and by study archetype: it is derived from a large global multi-biobank disease-focused study (many cohorts listed) with a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) and very large variant count (~1.09M), plus a larger validation sample (n=94,651) and multi-ancestry evaluation context. PGS004935 comes from a portability-style paper with single-cohort development (UKB), a much smaller variant set (6,127) consistent with a sparser framework score, and smaller validation (n=8,417). Effect-size evidence is similar-to-strong for both (OR ~1.5 vs ~1.66), so the broader, disease-focused multi-cohort support and genome-wide construction favor PGS005268.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar EUR-only development/evaluation, identical basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is discounted). Given this near-clone context, PGS000325 is better supported by stronger available performance signals: higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.76) and a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.51), plus slightly larger variant count (21 vs 12). Endpoint-wise both are JIA subtypes; neither is the exact umbrella ‘juvenile idiopathic arthritis’, so phenotype alignment does not clearly favor PGS000326 enough to offset PGS000325’s stronger discrimination/effect-size evidence.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to overall JIA, whereas PGS000324 is explicitly a subtype score (enthesitis-related JIA; phenotyping_reported = Enthesitis-related Arthritis), which is an endpoint-fidelity mismatch for a generic JIA target. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have the same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so the very high full-model AUROC for PGS000324 (0.93) is not sufficient to outweigh the subtype mismatch. PGS000114 also has slightly larger training (7,505 vs 5,354) and validation (940 vs 594), but the decision is primarily driven by endpoint alignment.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have identical basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, so endpoint fidelity to the broad target (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) is similarly subtype-specific rather than generic. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the best differentiators are the available discrimination proxies: PGS000324 shows materially stronger reported performance/effect evidence (full-model AUROC 0.93 with OR 3.09) than PGS000325 (AUROC 0.80, OR 1.93), and it also uses many more variants (138 vs 21), a positive structural signal within the same method family. PGS000325’s larger validation N (3,157 vs 594) is only a weak tie-break and doesn’t outweigh the stronger performance/effect-size and variant-count evidence for PGS000324.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it is from a kidney-cancer–focused, large multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) with a much larger variant set (107 vs 19) and a substantially stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5 vs PGS000076 HR 1.16), which is a key proxy for PRS discriminative power when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent (as they are for both). Both candidates only report full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.74 for PGS004908 vs 0.722 for PGS000076), which is not PRS-comparable and the small difference is not decisive; covariate sets are similarly epidemiologic (age/sex/PCs plus BMI/smoking/hypertension), so neither has an obvious leakage advantage. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS000076 comes from a cross-cancer evaluation framework and uses an incident-only endpoint, while PGS004908 is a direct kidney cancer model with strong disease-specific discovery context and comparable EUR evaluation.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is a disease-focused, kidney-cancer GWAS meta-analysis score with a much stronger PRS signal proxy (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) and a substantially richer variant set (107 genome-wide significant SNPs) than PGS000787 (19 variants; HR 1.15, 1.07–1.24 suggesting weak PRS discrimination). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R², so their similar full-model AUROCs (0.74 vs 0.722) are not decisive and are covariate-influenced in both (age/sex/PCs plus BMI/smoking/hypertension). Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS000787 is from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration framework and uses an incident time-to-event endpoint, whereas PGS004908 is directly framed as kidney cancer/renal carcinoma susceptibility from a dedicated kidney cancer GWAS study, making it the more reliable standalone PRS choice despite EUR-only evaluation.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported kidney cancer; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. Still, PGS000787 has stronger supporting evidence on the visible record: it reports an HR per SD (1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.24) indicating measurable PRS signal, and it uses a slightly larger variant set (19 vs 15). PGS000722 provides no effect-size evidence and only a modest full-model AUROC (0.567) with minimal covariate description, offering less support for PRS contribution. Validation sizes are similar and not decisive.

PGS000076 has stronger endpoint fidelity and more informative PRS signal evidence on the record: its trait_efo is renal cell carcinoma (the clinically dominant subtype of kidney cancer) and phenotyping is explicitly incident kidney cancer, plus it reports an HR per SD (1.16, 95% CI 1.08–1.26) and a C-index alongside AUROC. In contrast, PGS004690 is a single-record UKB/FinnGen-derived model with covariates listed as unknown and only a modest full-model AUROC (0.5644) with no PRS-only metrics or effect sizes, making its discrimination evidence less interpretable as PRS-driven. Both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and are EUR-only, so the decision rests on endpoint/phenotype clarity and available PRS-relevant effect-size support, favoring PGS000076.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (N18 chronic renal failure mapped to kidney failure), ancestry (EUR-only dev/eval), cohorts (UKB), training size (n=174,489) and validation size (n=56,192), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only ORs). With metrics otherwise absent, the main differentiator is the reported effect size: PGS004562 shows a materially stronger OR per SD (1.395) than PGS004492 (1.171), indicating stronger PRS signal on the same phenotype/context. Although PGS004492 uses LDpred2 (a strong shrinkage method), within the same publication/endpoint family the stronger empirical discrimination signal (OR) is the better-supported choice here.

PGS000787 is better supported on the visible fields because it provides clearer endpoint fidelity and more interpretable PRS contribution evidence: it targets renal cell carcinoma (the dominant subtype of kidney cancer) with an explicit incident kidney cancer phenotype and reports a PRS effect size (HR=1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.24). Although its AUROC/R² are full-model and covariate-influenced, the covariates are explicitly listed and are standard epidemiologic adjustments. In contrast, PGS004690 is a UKB/FinnGen-based framework-style cancer risk prediction score with unknown covariates and only a modest full-model AUROC (0.5644) and no PRS-only metrics or effect sizes, making its reported performance harder to interpret as PRS signal. Both are EUR-only and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the decision rests on endpoint/phenotype clarity and presence of PRS-specific effect evidence, favoring PGS000787.

Both candidates have essentially identical endpoint fidelity for the target trait (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), identical EUR-only ancestry context, identical covariates, identical variant count (19), and nearly identical full-model discrimination/effect size (AUROC ~0.722; HR per SD 1.16 for PGS000076 vs 1.15 for PGS000787). However, PGS000787 is explicitly derived from PGS000076 with inverse variant weights, which is a red-flag structural change with no compensating PRS-only performance evidence (no PGS-only AUC/R2 for either). The extra reported R²=0.366 in PGS000787 appears to be a full-model/other metric and is not PRS-comparable, and it is implausibly high relative to the provided kidney-cancer heritability ceiling, so it should not drive selection. Given PGS000076 is the original, directly specified GWAS-hits score with slightly stronger HR and more validation records (record_count 3 vs 1), it is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS000076 and PGS000722 both match the target well (trait_reported kidney cancer; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL; same GWAS-hits method family). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator; however, PGS000076 has materially stronger reported discrimination in its selected validation record (AUROC 0.722 with supporting C-index 0.724 and HR per SD 1.16), whereas PGS000722 reports a much lower AUROC (0.567) and no effect-size evidence. Although PGS000076 uses more covariates (age/sex/PCs plus standard risk factors) which can inflate full-model AUROC, PGS000722’s AUROC is still weak despite minimal covariates, and PGS000076 also has a larger variant set (19 vs 15) and richer performance reporting (multiple records). Overall, PGS000076 is better-supported on the visible evidence.

PGS004562 is the better match to the target trait “kidney failure” on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is explicitly kidney failure and its phenotyping_reported is ICD code N18 (chronic renal failure), which is closer to failure/ESRD than the broader CKD framing in PGS004158 (trait_efo: chronic kidney disease; phenotyping: “CKD or dialysis”). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so PGS004158’s reported AUROC/R² are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence; effect sizes are similar (OR ~1.39 for both). With metrics essentially non-differentiating, the decision falls to phenotype alignment, where PGS004562 is more directly aligned to kidney failure than PGS004158.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal carcinoma). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the similar full-model AUROCs (PGS000722=0.567 with CI vs PGS004690=0.5644) are not a reliable differentiator, especially with different/unknown covariates. Structurally, PGS004690 is better supported as a standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (AnnoPred) with ~6.35M variants and has explicit training sample size (n=367,502), whereas PGS000722 is a sparse GWAS-hits score (15 variants) with training size listed as N/A. Although PGS000722 has much larger validation n (400,812 vs 40,841) and cleaner disclosed covariate (genotyping array vs unknown), validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the large methodological/coverage advantage of PGS004690 given the lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

PGS004562 is the better match to the target trait kidney failure on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is explicitly "kidney failure" and phenotyping_reported is ICD code N18 (chronic renal failure), which is closer to kidney failure than PGS002237’s "chronic kidney disease (stage 3 or greater)" defined by eGFR<45 (a CKD severity threshold, not kidney failure). Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance metrics cannot cleanly differentiate; PGS002237’s AUROC=0.78 is a full-model metric and is further confounded by a heavy covariate set (hypertension, diabetes, BMI, medication use, etc.), making it less comparable to standalone PRS quality. While PGS002237 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and a slightly stronger OR (1.47 vs 1.40), the phenotype mismatch to kidney failure and covariate-heavy packaging outweigh those advantages given the lack of PRS-only metrics.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it is disease-focused (kidney cancer GWAS meta-analysis identifying susceptibility regions) with direct endpoint alignment (phenotyping_reported: “Kidney cancer”) and provides stronger PRS-relevant evidence via an effect size (OR=1.5 per SD) plus a substantially higher reported AUROC (0.74, albeit full-model with covariates). It also uses a much larger variant set (107 vs 15) and has a clear large European validation (n=324,805). In contrast, PGS000722 comes from a cross-cancer utility paper, uses a very sparse 15-variant GWAS-hits score, reports only a modest full-model AUROC (0.567) with minimal covariate detail (“Genotyping array”), and provides no effect-size evidence. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the decision relies on endpoint fidelity + study archetype + structural/effect-size support, favoring PGS004908.

PGS004492 is the better match to the target trait (kidney failure): its trait_efo is explicitly "kidney failure" and phenotyping_reported is ICD-10 N18 chronic renal failure, which is closer to failure/ESRD than candidate_b’s broader "chronic kidney disease" mapping. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so candidate_b’s reported AUROC/R² are full-model and not comparable as standalone PRS evidence; thus they don’t outweigh endpoint fidelity. Structurally, PGS004492 also has a much larger training sample (174,489 vs 13,496) and uses a standard genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2), while candidate_b is a benchmarking/ensemble-style score with mixed-ancestry evaluation but no PRS-only metrics. Overall, PGS004492 has stronger endpoint alignment and a cleaner disease-focused signal given the available fields.

PGS000708 is the better match to the target trait kidney failure: both trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly “Kidney failure,” and phenotyping_reported is a kidney-failure endpoint (diabetic kidney failure), whereas PGS004158 targets the broader CKD construct (“Chronic kidney disease (CKD)” with phenotyping “Chronic kidney disease or dialysis”), which is less endpoint-faithful to kidney failure specifically. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/C-index values are not directly comparable as PRS metrics; however, PGS000708 at least reports a time-to-event effect size (HR 1.19 per SD) with basic covariates, while PGS004158 provides only full-model AUROC/R² with covariates listed as 0 but on a broader phenotype. Given the primary importance of endpoint fidelity and the lack of clean PRS-only metrics in both, the exact kidney-failure alignment of PGS000708 outweighs PGS004158’s larger variant count and mixed-ancestry evaluation.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to kidney cancer/renal carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. PGS004908 is better supported overall: it comes from a kidney-cancer-focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (BBJ, FinnGen, NCI) with a much larger European validation sample (n=324,805) and provides an effect size (OR per SD=1.5, strong signal) plus clearly stated covariates (age, sex, PCs, BMI, smoking, hypertension), making the performance context more interpretable. PGS004690 is from a cross-cancer clinical+genetic risk prediction paper with unknown covariates and shows only a modest full-model AUROC (0.5644) without PRS-isolated metrics or effect sizes, so its standalone PRS strength is less evidenced despite using a genome-wide method (AnnoPred).

PGS004492 is the better-supported match to the target trait (kidney failure) on endpoint fidelity: its phenotyping_reported is ICD code N18 chronic renal failure, which aligns directly with kidney failure as a general endpoint, whereas PGS000708’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly restricted to “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a narrower subtype/etiology mismatch for a generic kidney failure target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000708’s full-model C-index=0.779 (with age/sex/PCs) is not a comparable PRS metric and cannot outweigh the phenotype mismatch. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural signals mildly favor PGS004492 as well (genome-wide LDpred2 with ~1.06M variants vs snpnet multi-PRS with 183k), while effect sizes are similarly modest (OR~1.17 vs HR~1.19).

PGS000708 is the better match to the target trait kidney failure on endpoint fidelity: its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly kidney failure and the phenotyping_reported is a kidney-failure endpoint (diabetic kidney failure), whereas PGS002237 targets chronic kidney disease stage ≥3 (eGFR<45), which is related but not kidney failure. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the similar full-model discrimination (C-index/AUROC ~0.78) is not a reliable differentiator; in that setting, PGS000708 also has cleaner covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch) than PGS002237’s heavier clinical/treatment covariate set, making its reported performance less likely to be covariate-inflated. PGS002237’s multi-ancestry evaluation is supportive for transportability, but it does not outweigh the endpoint mismatch and covariate comparability concerns versus the exact kidney-failure-aligned PGS000708.

PGS002237 is better supported for the target concept of kidney failure because its endpoint is a clearly defined severe CKD threshold (stage ≥3; eGFR <45), which is closer to progression toward kidney failure than PGS004158’s broader/less specific “CKD or dialysis” phenotype. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC values are not cleanly comparable; however, PGS002237 shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.47 vs 1.39) and is from a disease-focused across-ancestries CKD prediction study with explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation, whereas PGS004158 comes from a methods-evaluation/benchmarking paper with a smaller training set and limited evaluation ancestries. Despite PGS002237 using many clinical covariates (which inflates full-model AUROC), the overall endpoint fidelity + effect-size evidence favors it over PGS004158.

PGS002237 is better supported for the kidney-failure spectrum because it has clearer disease-focused endpoint definition and broader external evaluation context: phenotyping is explicitly CKD stage ≥3 (eGFR<45), and it reports multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE) with multiple performance records plus a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.47, CI 1.32–1.65). PGS004492 maps to kidney failure via ICD N18 chronic renal failure (reasonable alignment) and uses a strong genome-wide method (LDpred2, ~1.06M variants) with larger single-ancestry validation N, but it provides only a weak effect size (OR ~1.17) and no discrimination metrics or covariate transparency, making its empirical support thinner than PGS002237 despite the closer trait_efo label.

PGS000326 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint is a core JIA subtype (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) that aligns closely with the umbrella disease concept, whereas PGS000324 targets a narrower subtype (enthesitis-related JIA) that is less representative of generic JIA risk. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have the same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so the very high full-model AUROC for PGS000324 is discounted as non-PRS-comparable). With comparable study context, PGS000326’s broader phenotype fidelity to overall JIA outweighs PGS000324’s higher full-model AUROC/OR and higher variant count, which are not clean standalone-PRS evidence here.

PGS004562 is better aligned to the target trait as a general kidney failure endpoint: it uses ICD code N18 “Chronic renal failure” for both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported, which maps cleanly to kidney failure. It also shows a stronger PRS effect size (OR=1.395 per SD, moderate) than PGS000708 (HR=1.19, weak-to-moderate). In contrast, PGS000708 has an explicit phenotype restriction (“Diabetic kidney failure in all”), making it a narrower subtype and less faithful to generic kidney failure, and its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index=0.779 with covariates (age/sex/PCs), which is not PRS-comparable and cannot substitute for PGS-only performance. Both are EUR-only UKB-based with no PGS-only AUC/R2, so endpoint fidelity and effect size drive the decision.

PGS002729 is better supported for the target trait because it is a disease-focused knee osteoarthritis score with clear clinical endpoint description (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to knee OA; phenotyping_reported: “Clinical osteoarthritis”), explicit covariates (age, sex, BMI), and an actual reported discrimination metric in validation (full-model AUROC 0.66 with CI) across multiple development cohorts and a defined EUR evaluation set (n=14,926). In contrast, PGS004549 uses an ICD-style label (“M17 Gonarthrosis”) and a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with unknown covariates and provides no AUC/R2 at all (only a single OR=1.37), making its PRS performance and comparability much less evidenced despite larger training/validation N and genome-wide variant count.

PGS002729 is the better-supported knee osteoarthritis PRS on visible fields because it has the most endpoint-faithful, disease-focused framing (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: clinical knee osteoarthritis) and provides an explicit discrimination result (AUROC 0.66 with CI) with disclosed covariates (age, sex, BMI), even though this appears to be a full-model AUROC rather than PRS-only. In contrast, PGS004479 uses an ICD-style label (M17 gonarthrosis) and a strong genome-wide method/variant count (LDpred2; ~1.06M variants) with larger training/validation, but it lacks any AUC/R2 (PRS-only or otherwise) and reports only a moderate OR (~1.32) with unknown covariates, leaving its predictive performance and comparability less directly supported in the record.

PGS002767 is the better-supported standalone PRS for the generic target “knee osteoarthritis” because its endpoint is a direct disease status match (“Knee osteoarthritis”) without time-to-event/incident-only packaging, whereas PGS004883 explicitly targets “Incident knee osteoarthritis” and reports a time-to-event effect size (HR) plus only a full-model C-index/AUC (~0.60) that is not PRS-comparable. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the comparison leans on endpoint fidelity and PRS signal proxies: both have similar per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.35 for PGS002767 vs HR 1.37 for PGS004883; both moderate), but PGS002767 avoids the incident-only mismatch and uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/technical), while PGS004883’s reported discrimination is full-model and its training metadata (samples_training n=404; 1000G listed) adds little confidence. Overall, PGS002767 is the cleaner match to the target phenotype with comparably strong PRS signal evidence.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for knee osteoarthritis (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), same publication, same EUR-only training/evaluation context (UKB; n=174,489 train; n=56,192 validation), same variant count, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 or covariates—so performance metrics cannot differentiate. The main visible differentiator is effect size and model structure: PGS004549 (RFDiseasemetaPRS) shows a higher per-SD OR (1.3667) than PGS004479 (LDpred2; OR 1.3233), and its method name indicates a meta/ensemble-style integration (a positive structural signal when other fields are tied). Therefore PGS004549 is better supported on the available evidence.

PGS002767 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (knee osteoarthritis) because its endpoint fidelity is a direct match: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Knee osteoarthritis,” aligned with the target and the same EFO term as the comparator. PGS004479 maps to the same EFO but uses an ICD-style label (“M17 Gonarthrosis”), which is close but slightly less direct for the stated target wording. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can only be weakly compared via effect size; PGS002767 shows a slightly higher OR per SD (1.35 with CI 1.3–1.4) than PGS004479 (OR ~1.323 without CI), giving it marginally stronger and cleaner performance evidence. Additionally, PGS002767 discloses standard, non-leaky covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), whereas PGS004479 has covariates listed as unknown, lowering interpretability. Although PGS004479 has larger training and validation N, those are weak tie-breakers here and do not outweigh the clearer endpoint/covariate documentation and slightly stronger OR evidence in PGS002767.

Both candidates are near-clones: same late-onset Alzheimer’s disease endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo) and identical phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (GWAS-significant variants) with the same 21 variants, same covariates (age, sex), same publication and development cohorts, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2. With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the reported PRS effect size: PGS000054 shows a materially stronger OR per SD (1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is stronger evidence of discriminative signal. Although PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-on-EUR evaluation, validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger effect size in PGS000054; PGS000054’s AMR evaluation also provides some transportability evidence rather than being a clear weakness.

Both candidates match the target trait (knee osteoarthritis) at trait_reported/trait_efo, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model discrimination is not a clean PRS comparator. PGS002729 is better supported as a disease-focused, multi-cohort OA score (training/development cohorts span multiple OA resources/biobanks) with a broadly clinical endpoint (“Clinical osteoarthritis”) and a reasonable full-model AUROC 0.66 (age/sex/BMI covariates). In contrast, PGS004883 comes from a pan-disease incidence framework (“country-specific cumulative incidence for 18 diseases”), uses an incident time-to-event endpoint, and shows only modest full-model C-index 0.60 with HR 1.37 (moderate signal) plus a weak/odd development context (training n=404; cohort listed as 1000G), making it look more like a framework-derived score with less direct disease-specific support. Validation N is larger for PGS004883, but that is a weak tie-break and doesn’t outweigh the stronger disease-focused multi-cohort context of PGS002729.

PGS004549 is better supported for the target knee osteoarthritis because it has strong endpoint fidelity (ICD-10 M17 gonarthrosis explicitly mapping to knee OA, with trait_efo also knee OA) and comes from a disease-prediction study explicitly integrating disease PRS with risk-factor PRS, with a much larger training set (n=174,489 UKB) and larger validation (n=56,192) than PGS004883. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics can’t cleanly differentiate; however PGS004549 provides a comparable per-SD effect size (OR=1.37) similar to PGS004883’s HR=1.37, while PGS004883’s only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index=0.6 (not PRS-comparable) and it is framed as a country-specific cumulative incidence/time-to-event framework with incident-only phenotyping, which is a mild endpoint/packaging penalty versus a direct diagnosis-code endpoint. Ancestry is EUR-only for both, so no advantage there.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target via trait_efo (osteoarthritis, knee) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance metrics don’t differentiate beyond similar per-SD ORs (PGS002767 OR=1.35 with CI; PGS004549 OR≈1.37 without CI). PGS004549 is better-supported on study development evidence: it reports a concrete training sample size (n=174,489) and a specified development cohort (UKB), and uses an explicit meta/ensemble-style method (RFDiseasemetaPRS) which is a positive structural signal versus PGS002767’s single-score PRS-CS in a cross-disease comparison paper. PGS002767 has slightly cleaner covariate disclosure (age/sex/PCs/technical) and a more direct plain-language phenotype label, but overall the stronger development documentation and aggregation method give PGS004549 the edge.

PGS002767 is the better-supported standalone PRS for knee osteoarthritis: it has exact endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported = "Knee osteoarthritis" matching the target) and provides a PRS-specific effect size (OR per SD 1.35, 95% CI 1.30–1.40), with only basic demographic/PC/technical covariates. In contrast, PGS002729 uses a less specific endpoint label (phenotyping_reported = "Clinical osteoarthritis" rather than knee-specific) and its only visible discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.66 adjusted for Age/sex/BMI (not PRS-only and thus not comparable), while also being a very sparse 24-variant GWS score. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the combination of tighter phenotype alignment plus genome-wide shrinkage construction and PRS-specific OR evidence favors PGS002767.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease in trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported). However, PGS000054 has cleaner and more interpretable PRS evidence via a strong reported effect size (OR=1.73 per SD, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) with only basic covariates (age, sex), and it is developed across many Alzheimer’s-focused cohorts with external evaluation in an AMR (Hispanic/Latin American) sample (n=3,324), supporting transportability beyond EUR. PGS000334 reports only a generic R²=0.191 that appears to be a full-model/unspecified metric (top-level PRS-only R² is null) with unknown covariates, making the performance less comparable and potentially inflated; it is also evaluated only in EUR (n=3,810). Given the stronger, cleaner PRS signal and clearer covariate context, PGS000054 is better supported.

PGS000054 is the better-supported late-onset Alzheimer’s disease PRS on the visible fields: it has clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported explicitly late-onset/familial LOAD) and provides PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.73, strong signal) with basic covariates (age, sex) and a substantially larger external evaluation sample (n=3,324) in an AMR/Hispanic evaluation context. In contrast, PGS004918 is a pathway-restricted score (8 SNPs in synaptic-function genes) with very small development/validation (samples_training n=439; validation n=136), unknown covariates, and only a full-model AUROC (0.731) which is not PRS-comparable and cannot substitute for PGS-only performance; it also narrows the construct beyond generic LOAD risk. Overall, PGS000054 has stronger disease-focused evidence and more informative PRS-specific performance support than PGS004918.

PGS004479 is better supported as a standalone knee osteoarthritis PRS: it has coherent endpoint mapping to knee OA via ICD-style code M17 (gonarthrosis) with matching trait_efo, and it is developed/trained in a large UKB sample (n=174,489) with a large genome-wide shrinkage model (LDpred2; ~1.06M variants) and moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.32). PGS004883 has an exact label and incident endpoint, but it comes from a pan-disease absolute-incidence framework paper and reports only a full-model C-index/AUC=0.60 (not PRS-only) alongside HR=1.37; its listed training sample is extremely small (n=404) and development cohort is 1000G, making the evidence package look more like a framework/packaging artifact than a disease-optimized PRS. With neither candidate providing PRS-only AUC/R2, the stronger disease-focused development signal and larger, more plausible training context favor PGS004479.

PGS000054 has stronger endpoint fidelity to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease: its phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Familial late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD)” and it reports a direct disease-risk effect size (OR=1.73 per SD, 95% CI 1.57–1.93), which is meaningful PRS discrimination evidence even without AUC/R2. PGS000053 is the better-supported late-onset Alzheimer’s disease PRS on endpoint fidelity and PRS-relevant evidence. Both candidates map to the same EFO and are EUR-only, but PGS000053 targets a straightforward disease endpoint (“Alzheimer's disease (late onset)”; phenotyping: “Familial late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD)”) with basic covariates (age, sex) and has a substantially larger evaluation sample (n=4,792) plus a PRS-relevant effect size (OR=1.29 per SD, with CI). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the stronger disease-focused evidence package and effect-size support favor PGS000053.

Both candidates match the target trait well (lung cancer/lung carcinoma; incident lung cancer), have identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariate bundles (including smoking variables and family history), identical validation size (n=392,539), and essentially identical full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) and HR per SD (~1.16–1.17). Its additional reported R²=0.799 is a generic/full-model metric (not PRS-only) and is also implausibly high relative to the lung-cancer heritability ceiling provided, making it non-informative or suspect for PRS ranking. Therefore PGS000078 is better-supported on the visible fields as the primary, non-derived score.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and both use C+T with unknown covariates, so endpoint fidelity and covariate comparability don’t separate them. PGS004860 is the better-supported match to the generic target trait “lung cancer” because its endpoint fidelity is higher: phenotyping_reported is “Incident lung cancer,” whereas PGS000740 is explicitly restricted to “Early onset lung cancer (< 50 years),” a narrower, age-conditioned subtype that is a mismatch for a broad lung cancer target. PGS000334 has much better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is directly “Late-onset Alzheimer’s disease,” matching trait_reported/trait_efo. PGS000078 is better aligned to the generic target trait “lung cancer” because its phenotyping is “Incident lung cancer,” whereas PGS000740 is restricted to “Early onset lung cancer (< 50 years),” an age-conditioned subtype that is a poorer match for general lung cancer risk. PGS000789 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target trait “lung cancer” via an incident lung cancer phenotype, whereas PGS000740 is explicitly restricted to early-onset lung cancer (<50 years), a narrower endpoint mismatch for a general lung cancer target. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.846 for PGS000789 vs 0.811 for PGS000740) are not cleanly comparable and are likely covariate-influenced; however PGS000789 at least provides a PRS-linked effect size (HR=1.17) while PGS000740 provides no effect sizes in the visible fields. PGS004860 is better supported structurally and by endpoint specificity: it targets lung carcinoma with an explicit incident lung cancer endpoint and uses a genome-wide LDpred2 model with ~1.14M variants, which is generally more appropriate for a polygenic architecture than PGS000721’s 19 genome-wide significant SNPs. Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are all lung cancer / incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS and EUR evaluation). Although PGS000078 has much larger validation n, validation size is a weak tie-breaker and does not outweigh the method/variant-count and effect-size advantage for PGS004860.

PGS000754 is the better-supported match to the target trait (lupus erythematosus) because its phenotyping_reported is the general systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosis, whereas PGS000328 is explicitly restricted to early-onset SLE (onset before age 20), which is a narrower endpoint mismatch for a generic lupus target. Both candidates map cleanly to systemic lupus erythematosus (same trait_reported and trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.83 for PGS000328 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) are not strong, comparable differentiators. Both candidates align on the target disease concept (trait_reported/trait_efo = systemic lupus erythematosus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS003960 (0.89 vs 0.79) is not a reliable PRS discriminator—especially because PGS003960 explicitly includes a phenotype risk score covariate, a strong clinical-packaging/leakage signal that can inflate full-model AUROC and makes the metric non-comparable to standalone PRS performance. Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported all systemic lupus erythematosus), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS003960’s very high full-model AUROC (0.89) is explicitly conditioned on a “phenotype risk score” covariate, which is strong clinical/EHR packaging and makes the metric largely non-comparable to standalone PRS quality.
