Given the heavy covariate leakage signal in PGS003960 and the stronger structural PRS construction in PGS000754, PGS000754 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS004918 has better endpoint fidelity to the target late-onset Alzheimer’s disease: its phenotyping_reported is a direct “Late-onset Alzheimer’s disease,” whereas PGS002289’s phenotyping_reported is a cognitive test performance age-interaction outcome (not AD diagnosis), making it more of a cognition/aging proxy than the target disease endpoint. Both candidates match the target well at the concept level (trait_reported/trait_efo are systemic lupus erythematosus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.65 for PGS000754 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) are not cleanly comparable PRS evidence. Although PGS000196 has a higher reported full-model AUROC, it comes from a much smaller validation sample (n=245 vs n=7,733) and a more clinically contextual phenotype, so PGS000754 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported all systemic lupus erythematosus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (PGS004917 0.696 vs PGS000754 0.65) is not a reliable differentiator. PGS000754 also has broader evaluation ancestry mix (ASN/EAS/EUR) and larger validation N (7,733 vs 3,945), while PGS004917’s publication focus on smoking interactions raises mild risk of non-generalizable packaging even though covariates are listed as unknown. Overall, PGS000754 has the stronger general-purpose PRS evidence package given the lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported all systemic lupus erythematosus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as PRS performance. Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease in trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported) and neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R². PGS000334 lacks any PRS effect size, has covariates listed as unknown, and its only quantitative metric is an R²=0.191 reported under other_metrics/full-model context (not PRS-only), which is hard to interpret and potentially inflated/non-comparable given the heritability ceiling guidance. Both candidates align to the target trait at the concept level (trait_reported/trait_efo are systemic lupus erythematosus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (PGS000328=0.83 vs PGS004917=0.696) are not directly comparable PRS metrics. Overall, PGS004917 is better supported for generic lupus risk despite the lower full-model AUROC.

Both candidates align well to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo are systemic lupus erythematosus), but PGS000196’s phenotyping is narrower/packaged to an arthritis outpatient context (“SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis”), making endpoint fidelity less clean for generic lupus erythematosus risk than PGS004917’s straightforward “systemic lupus erythematosus” phenotyping. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a reliable differentiator; however PGS004917 adds supportive PRS signal via effect sizes (OR 2.01 per SD, β 0.7) that PGS000196 lacks. PGS004917 also has a much larger validation sample (n=3,945 vs n=245), which modestly increases trust once endpoints are acceptable. Overall, PGS004917 is better supported on endpoint generality plus effect-size evidence, despite its slightly lower full-model AUROC.

PGS000078 is better supported for the target trait (lung cancer) because it has stronger overall evidence despite both candidates lacking PRS-only AUC/R2. Endpoint alignment is good for both, but PGS000078 specifies an incident lung cancer endpoint, reports an effect size (HR per SD 1.16, 95% CI 1.11–1.22) providing some PRS-specific signal, and uses a much larger variant set (109 vs 19) within the same GWAS-significant-variants method family. PGS000721 has a smaller validation sample (n=1,202 vs n=392,539) and its reported AUROC (0.738) is a full-model metric with clinical covariates including lung-function ratio (FEV1/FVC), which is closer to a mediator/near-outcome predictor and makes the discrimination less attributable to the PRS; it also provides no PRS effect size. PGS000078 also has heavy covariates (including smoking variables and family history), so its high full-model AUROC (0.846) is not treated as PRS-comparable, but overall it still has the stronger, more coherent support package than PGS000721.

PGS000053 has stronger endpoint fidelity to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease: its phenotyping_reported is a direct disease endpoint (“Familial late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD)”) with basic covariates (age, sex) and it reports a PRS-relevant effect size (OR per SD 1.29, 95% CI 1.21–1.37), giving at least some direct evidence of discriminative signal. In contrast, PGS002289—despite a much larger validation sample—appears primarily evaluated on a cognitive test performance interaction phenotype (“Pairs matching… x age interaction”) with only an indirect cognition-based metric and unknown covariates, making it less aligned with the target disease endpoint and less comparable as a disease-risk PRS. Both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so phenotype alignment and PRS-relevant effect-size evidence favor PGS000053.

Both candidates match the target trait (lung cancer / lung carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the listed AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as PRS performance. Endpoint fidelity favors PGS000721 because its phenotyping_reported is generic “Lung cancer,” whereas PGS000740 is restricted to “Early onset lung cancer (< 50 years),” a narrower endpoint than the target. Although PGS000740 has many more variants (128 vs 19) and much larger validation (167,955 vs 1,202) with some AFR evaluation, its reported model is heavily packaged with additional clinical predictors including family history and personal history of cancer, making its full-model AUROC (0.811) especially non-informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS000721 uses more standard lung-cancer risk covariates (including smoking status) and keeps the endpoint aligned to overall lung cancer, so it is the better-supported match despite weaker scale.

PGS000077 is the better-supported lymphoid leukemia PRS: it matches the target EFO and uses a direct incident lymphocytic leukemia endpoint, reports a meaningful PRS effect size (HR=1.45 per SD) and provides transparent, basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs) with a very large EUR validation sample (n=391,338). PGS002305 is also endpoint-aligned (chronic lymphoid leukemia) but has weaker visible support: lower reported full-model AUROC (0.57 vs 0.719, noting neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2), no effect-size evidence, unknown covariates, and a much smaller validation sample (n=265).

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia), but PGS000077 has stronger endpoint fidelity via an explicit incident diagnosis phenotype ("Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia") and is supported by a multi-cohort development context (multiple listed training/development cohorts) with a much larger evaluation sample (n=391,338 vs n=957). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator; however, PGS000077 shows a stronger per-SD effect size (HR=1.45) than PGS000645’s OR=1.358, and PGS000645 is an extremely sparse P+T score (6 variants) with modest full-model AUROC (0.578). Overall, PGS000077 has the more robust evidence package despite lacking PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia; phenotyping_reported=Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), with no PRS-only AUC/R² reported for either. However, PGS000788 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000077 (“75 variants from Graff et al (PGS000077) with inverse variant weights”), which is a strong packaging/red-flag signal: it is not an independently developed PRS for the endpoint and the inverted weights make its apparent full-model AUROC/HR differences hard to interpret as better PRS evidence. PGS000077 is the original genome-wide-significant 75-variant score with coherent development cohorts listed and multiple validation records, making it the better-supported primary model on the visible metadata despite PGS000788’s slightly higher full-model AUROC/HR.

PGS000328 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint is explicitly restricted to “Systemic lupus erythematosus (onset before age 20)”, which is a clear, diagnosis-anchored SLE phenotype without disclosed non-genetic packaging, whereas PGS003960’s evaluation is explicitly adjusted for a “phenotype risk score” covariate—an EHR-derived clinical/phenotypic risk package that strongly inflates and de-comparabilizes the reported full-model AUROC (0.89) and provides little evidence about standalone PRS performance. Both candidates target the same EFO trait (systemic lupus erythematosus), use similar GWAS-hits methods with the same variant count (57), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the key differentiator is covariate leakage risk: PGS000328 has unknown covariates (less concerning than explicit phenotype-risk-score augmentation), making it the cleaner PRS candidate despite smaller validation (1,001 vs 3,048) and a lower full-model AUROC (0.83 vs 0.89).

PGS000788 is better supported for the target lymphoid leukemia because its endpoint is explicitly incident lymphocytic leukemia (direct clinical disease endpoint) and it shows a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.7, 95% CI 1.53–1.88) with only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), suggesting meaningful PRS signal. Although its reported AUROC/R² are full-model (not PRS-only) and thus not directly comparable, PGS000645 also lacks PRS-only metrics and has weaker overall performance evidence (full-model AUROC 0.578; OR per SD 1.358) plus an extremely sparse 6-variant P+T score developed in a single cohort (MGI, n=1,100). With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R², the stronger effect-size evidence and more substantial variant set favor PGS000788 despite PGS000645’s exact trait label match.

PGS000788 is better supported for the broad target of lymphoid leukemia: its phenotyping is an incident lymphocytic leukemia endpoint (broader/less subtype-restricted than PGS002305’s chronic lymphoid leukemia), it reports a strong PRS-associated effect size (HR per SD 1.7, suggesting meaningful discrimination even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent), and it uses clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs) without obvious clinical-risk packaging. PGS002305 has a narrower CLL-only endpoint, unknown covariates (reducing interpretability/comparability), and only a modest full-model AUROC (0.57) with no PRS-only metrics or effect sizes to isolate PRS contribution. Both are EUR-evaluated and lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint generality plus effect-size evidence favors PGS000788.

PGS003453 is more endpoint-faithful to the target trait (lymphoid leukemia) because it targets chronic lymphocytic leukemia (a specific lymphoid leukemia subtype) with matching phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS000077 is a broader “Lymphocytic leukemia” score evaluated as incident-only and comes from a cross-cancer evaluation context. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so discrimination must lean on effect sizes: PGS003453 shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR=2.17) than PGS000077 (HR=1.45), supporting better PRS signal. PGS000077 has cleaner/basic covariates and much larger validation n, but its only AUROC is full-model (0.719) and thus not PRS-comparable; with no PRS-only metrics, the stronger disease-specific effect size and tighter phenotype alignment make PGS003453 better supported overall.

PGS000645 is the better match to the target trait (lymphoid leukemia): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align exactly to lymphoid leukemia, whereas PGS003453 is specifically chronic lymphocytic leukemia (a subtype) and thus has weaker endpoint fidelity for the broader target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so discrimination can’t be compared cleanly; PGS003453 does show a stronger per-SD OR (2.17 vs 1.36 for PGS000645), but it also has unknown covariates and no training/development cohort metadata, making its evidence package less interpretable. Given the primary importance of phenotype alignment and the cleaner, explicitly basic covariate set in PGS000645 (age/sex/PCs/batch), PGS000645 narrowly wins despite weaker effect size and smaller validation.

PGS003453 is the better-supported match to the target trait (lymphoid leukemia) because it targets a specific lymphoid leukemia subtype with high endpoint fidelity: trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are both chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which is a clear lymphoid leukemia entity. It also reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.17 per SD), providing direct evidence of discriminative signal. In contrast, PGS000788 comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration context and its only discrimination metrics are full-model AUROC/C-index/R² (no PRS-only AUC/R²), making the apparent performance largely non-comparable for PRS ranking; additionally it is a reweighted derivative of another score rather than a primary disease-focused construction. While PGS000788 has a much larger EUR validation sample and broader GWAS ancestry mix, those are weak tie-breakers here given the stronger endpoint specificity and clearer PRS effect-size evidence for PGS003453.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all age-related macular degeneration), use the same method (PRS-CS), same basic covariates (age, sex, PCs 1–10), and have identical European evaluation context and validation sample size (n=163,011), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this near-clone setup, PGS004606 has stronger visible performance/effect evidence in the selected record: higher full-model AUROC (0.71 vs 0.65) and a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.76 vs 1.48). PGS004607 also has a GWAS ancestry mismatch (AFR GWAS but EUR evaluation) relative to PGS004606’s EUR→EUR alignment, which is a transportability advantage for PGS004606 in this head-to-head.

PGS003453 is a tighter endpoint match to the target trait (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported both explicitly chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a specific lymphoid leukemia subtype), whereas PGS002305 maps to the broader lymphoid leukemia EFO but is framed as a cross-cancer evaluation. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002305’s full-model AUROC=0.57 is not a comparable PRS metric and provides limited standalone PRS evidence. In that metric vacuum, PGS003453’s reported per-SD effect size (OR=2.17, 95% CI 2.07–2.28) is strong discriminative evidence, while PGS002305 provides no effect size and only a small validation (n=265) versus PGS003453’s much larger validation (n=20,134), which modestly increases trust. Both use the same sparse GWAS-significant 43-variant approach and EUR-only context, so the effect-size evidence and endpoint specificity favor PGS003453.

Both candidates align to the target trait (AMD) at trait_reported/trait_efo and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004952 (0.842) is not a reliable PRS-comparable advantage over PGS004606 (0.71). PGS004606 has stronger structural and PRS-signal evidence: a genome-wide PRS-CS model with ~1,000,946 variants and a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.76 vs 1.41 for PGS004952), plus far larger validation (n=163,011 vs n=1,232). PGS004952 also narrows the endpoint to late AMD clinical classification, which is slightly less faithful to the generic ‘macular degeneration’ target than PGS004606’s general AMD phenotyping. Overall, PGS004606 is better-supported as a standalone PRS.

PGS002246 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target trait melanoma: its phenotyping_reported is "Incident invasive melanoma," a direct clinical disease endpoint, whereas PGS000813 is restricted to "Familial cutaneous melanoma in non-carriers of a CDKN2A mutation," a special high-risk subgroup that may not generalize to overall melanoma risk. Both candidates are EUR-only and use similarly light covariates (age, sex) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000813 (0.77 vs 0.688) is not treated as a clean PRS advantage. With comparable method families (GWAS-significant variant sets; 46 vs 50 variants) and similar validation sizes, the more general, clinically aligned phenotype in PGS002246 is the stronger support.

PGS002305 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint is a clinically specific subtype (chronic lymphoid leukemia) that still maps to the same trait_efo (lymphoid leukemia) and it is developed/evaluated in a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort cancer PRS evaluation setting (many contributing cohorts listed), which is generally more reliable than a sparse single-biobank-style score. While both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so the similar full-model AUROC ~0.57 cannot differentiate), PGS002305 has a much richer genetic model (43 genome-wide significant variants) versus PGS000645’s extremely sparse 6-variant P+T score, and PGS000645’s evidence is further limited by small training (n=1,100) and a repository-style publication context. Covariates are unknown for PGS002305 (reducing confidence), but PGS000645’s reported full-model metrics with basic covariates still do not provide PRS-comparable performance, leaving structural/study-design signals to favor PGS002305.

PGS004952 is a tighter endpoint match to the target (explicit age-related macular degeneration; phenotyping_reported = late AMD clinical classification) and comes from a disease-focused AMD consortium context (IAMDGC), with supportive PRS effect size evidence (OR per SD 1.41). Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and only reports a covariate-influenced full-model AUROC (0.842 with age/sex/PCs), PGS001013’s clean PRS-only metrics are very weak (PGS-only AUROC 0.553; R2 0.006) and it is a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a broad/less specific phenotype (“Eye problems/disorders Macular degeneration”), which domain guidance flags as typically underperforming disease-focused models. Overall, endpoint fidelity and study archetype favor PGS004952 despite less directly comparable PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates match the target trait conceptually (AMD) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the very high full-model AUROC shown for PGS004952 (0.842) is not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator. Given that, PGS004607 has stronger structural and scale signals for a standalone PRS: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.07M variants and shows a slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.48 vs 1.41 for PGS004952). PGS004607 also uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and has much larger European validation (n=163,011 vs n=1,232), whereas PGS004952 is a sparse 52-SNP GWS score and its endpoint is specifically ‘Late AMD’ (more subtype-restricted than the generic AMD target). Overall, PGS004607 is better-supported for generic macular degeneration risk despite PGS004952’s higher full-model AUROC.

PGS004606 has much stronger endpoint fidelity for the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is the direct disease endpoint “Age-related macular degeneration,” whereas PGS002269’s phenotyping_reported is a proxy/biomarker trait (retinal photoreceptor layer thickness) despite sharing the AMD label. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be cleanly compared; however PGS004606 provides supportive disease-risk evidence via an OR=1.76 per SD and uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), while PGS002269 reports only a beta on the biomarker and includes additional exposure covariates (e.g., smoking) in a non-disease endpoint context. PGS004606 also has a stronger structural profile for a PRS (genome-wide PRS-CS with ~1,000,946 variants and large EUR validation n=163,011) versus PGS002269’s 47-variant score and smaller validation n=44,823.

PGS004607 is the better-supported choice for macular degeneration because its endpoint fidelity is direct (phenotyping_reported = Age-related macular degeneration) whereas PGS002269, despite the same trait label/EFO, is explicitly evaluated/anchored on a proxy biomarker phenotype (retinal/photoreceptor layer thickness), which is a weaker match for the target disease endpoint. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparability relies on secondary signals: PGS004607 reports an OR per SD of 1.48 (moderate-to-strong PRS signal) and uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), while PGS002269 reports a beta on retinal thickness (not directly interpretable as AMD risk discrimination) and includes additional exposure covariates (e.g., smoking). PGS004607 also has a more modern genome-wide shrinkage construction (PRS-CS; ~1.07M variants) and a large European evaluation sample (n=163,011), whereas PGS002269 is a sparse 47-variant score with less directly relevant validation context for AMD risk.

PGS004607 is a disease-focused, endpoint-faithful score explicitly for age-related macular degeneration (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all align) from a dedicated AMD across-ancestries GWAS study, and it shows a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.48, near the “strong” threshold) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a full-model AUROC=0.65, which is not PRS-comparable), its overall evidence package is more consistent with a high-quality AMD PRS than PGS001013, which comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”), uses only 53 variants, and has weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.553; R² 0.006) despite reporting metrics. PGS001013’s broader, self-reported ‘Eye problems/disorders’ phenotype and framework archetype make its metric advantage insufficient to outweigh PGS004607’s stronger endpoint fidelity and disease-focused design.

PGS004606 is a disease-focused, endpoint-faithful score for age-related macular degeneration (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all align) developed from an AMD consortium cohort (IAMDGC) with basic covariates only (age/sex/PCs) and shows strong PRS signal via OR=1.76 per SD in a large European validation (n=163,011). PGS001013, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.553, R2=0.006), comes from a pan-trait UKB sparse snpnet framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very small 53-variant model and a broader/less specific phenotype label (“Eye problems/disorders Macular degeneration”), and its PRS-only performance is modest. Given the strong endpoint fidelity + consortium disease-study archetype and stronger effect-size evidence, PGS004606 is better supported overall despite lacking explicit PGS-only AUROC/R2.

Both candidates are EUR-only GWAS-hits melanoma scores with no PRS-only AUC/R² reported, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. Endpoint fidelity favors PGS002246 because its phenotyping is explicitly "Incident invasive melanoma," a clear clinical endpoint, whereas PGS000743 is evaluated in a heavily covariate-packaged risk-factor model (includes pigmentation traits, nevi, sun exposure, keratinocyte cancer history, and family history), making its reported AUROC=0.74 likely dominated by non-genetic predictors and less informative about the PRS itself. PGS002246 uses only age and sex covariates (cleaner, less leakage) and has a larger validation sample (4,765 vs 1,035), providing more reliable external evaluation despite a lower full-model AUROC.

PGS002246 is the better-supported match to the target trait melanoma because its endpoint fidelity is cleaner (phenotyping_reported: incident invasive melanoma) and it comes from a melanoma-focused independent evaluation study, whereas PGS000424 is from a broader cancer PRS repository framework and uses a looser endpoint (diagnosis or history), which is closer to a survivorship/prevalent construct. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC/R² for PGS002246 (0.688; R² 0.07 with only age/sex covariates) is supportive but not decisive; still, it exceeds PGS000424’s full-model AUROC/R² (0.619; pseudo-R² 0.035) despite PGS000424’s larger training/validation sizes and inclusion of PCs/batch. Overall, the combination of more faithful incident endpoint and disease-focused external evaluation context favors PGS002246.

PGS004952 is better aligned to the target trait as a direct clinical AMD endpoint (phenotyping_reported: late age-related macular degeneration) whereas PGS002269’s phenotyping_reported is retinal photoreceptor layer thickness, an OCT biomarker/proxy rather than macular degeneration itself. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004952’s full-model AUROC=0.842 cannot be treated as PRS performance, but it at least provides some discrimination evidence alongside an OR=1.41; PGS002269 provides only a beta on the biomarker. Although PGS002269 has a much larger validation sample (n=44,823 vs n=1,232), validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the endpoint mismatch/proxy-phenotype issue.

PGS001013 is the better-supported PRS for the target trait (macular degeneration) because it uses a direct macular degeneration disease endpoint (phenotyping_reported: "Eye problems/disorders Macular degeneration") and provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.55283; PGS-only R2=0.00599) with basic covariates; its PRS-only R2 is also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS002269, despite a closer label (age-related macular degeneration) and a disease-focused publication context, has a phenotype mismatch in the visible fields (phenotyping_reported is retinal layer thickness—an OCT biomarker/proxy rather than AMD diagnosis) and reports no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only a beta effect size), making its PRS evidence less directly supportive for macular degeneration risk prediction.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo = melanoma; EUR GWAS/EVAL; similar sparse GWAS-hit style with 45–46 variants) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable. PGS000813 is better supported because it provides PRS-relevant effect size evidence (OR per SD 2.12 and top-10% vs middle-20% OR 5.7) in addition to a slightly higher reported AUROC (0.77 vs 0.74), and it uses relatively light covariates (age, sex) whereas PGS000743’s AUROC is paired with a very heavy traditional risk-factor set including family history and keratinocyte cancer history, making its full-model AUROC more likely covariate-driven and less informative about the PRS itself. Although PGS000813’s phenotyping is restricted to familial cutaneous melanoma in CDKN2A non-carriers (a narrower endpoint than PGS000743’s generic melanoma), the stronger PRS-specific effect-size reporting and cleaner covariate context outweigh that specificity concern.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (melanoma), same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication and validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not clean PRS-comparable). With endpoint and study context effectively identical, the only differentiators are small full-model metric differences (AUROC 0.691 vs 0.688; R² 0.072 vs 0.070—too small to matter) and structural variant count, where PGS002247 includes more genome-wide significant variants (68 vs 50), a modest within-method advantage. Hence PGS002247 edges PGS002246, but confidence is low due to the overall near-tie and lack of PRS-only metrics.

PGS002247 is the better-supported melanoma PRS on endpoint fidelity and overall evidence package: it targets a clean clinical endpoint (“Incident invasive melanoma”) with only basic covariates (age, sex) and comes from an independent evaluation in prospective UK and Australian cohorts, which is a stronger external-validation archetype than the repository-style Cancer PRSweb record for PGS000424 (“Melanomas of skin, dx or hx”). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable PRS metrics; however, PGS002247’s reported AUROC/R² (0.691/0.072) are higher than PGS000424’s (0.619/0.035) under similarly light covariate adjustment. PGS000424 does provide effect sizes and larger training/validation Ns, but it is a broader diagnosis-or-history phenotype and a framework/repository context, which is typically less reliable than a disease-focused independent evaluation when PRS-only metrics are absent.

PGS000813 is better supported for the target trait melanoma because its endpoint is a clinically specific melanoma subtype (familial cutaneous melanoma in non-carriers of CDKN2A) from a disease-focused multi-cohort context (multiple melanoma consortia/cohorts listed) and it shows stronger PRS signal via effect sizes (OR per SD 2.12; top 10% vs middle 20% OR 5.7). PGS000424 comes from a repository/framework-style cancer PRSweb evaluation (UKB-derived P+T) with weaker effect size evidence (OR per SD 1.56; top 1% vs rest OR 3.12) and only modest full-model AUROC (0.619). Neither reports PRS-only AUROC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000813 (0.77) is not decisive, but combined with the stronger ORs and disease-focused multi-cohort provenance it outweighs PGS000424’s larger single-biobank training/validation sizes.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Multiple myeloma; trait_efo = plasma cell myeloma) and are EUR-only, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. Still, PGS002281 comes from a disease-focused multiple-myeloma risk prediction paper and shows stronger validation evidence on the visible fields (higher full-model AUROC 0.644 with basic covariates age/sex/region, and a stronger extreme-risk contrast OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18) than PGS000653 (full-model AUROC 0.577; OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1). PGS000653 is from a broader cancer PRS repository framework context (Cancer PRSweb) and does not show stronger PRS-isolated metrics to offset its weaker discrimination/effect-size signals. Validation sample sizes are similar, so they don’t break the tie.

Both candidates map cleanly to melanoma (trait_efo=melanoma) and are EUR-only in GWAS/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). However, PGS000743’s reported AUROC=0.74 is explicitly tied to a very heavy covariate bundle including family history, pigmentation traits, nevi, sun exposure, and prior keratinocyte cancer—strong risk-factor packaging that makes the full-model AUROC largely non-informative for standalone PRS quality. In contrast, PGS000424 uses only basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), provides additional performance evidence (Nagelkerke R², Brier, OR top 1% vs rest, and per-SD OR=1.56), and has explicit training cohort context (UKB) with large validation (n=14,482). Given the much cleaner covariate context and richer PRS-relevant effect-size evidence, PGS000424 is better-supported than PGS000743 for melanoma PRS selection.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to melanoma (trait_reported/trait_efo match), use the same GWAS-hits method, and lack PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.74 for PGS000743 vs 0.691 for PGS002247) are not cleanly comparable—especially because PGS000743’s model includes extensive traditional risk factors and family history, making its AUROC likely covariate-driven. PGS002247 has cleaner covariates (age, sex only), a more deployment-relevant phenotype definition (“incident invasive melanoma”), a substantially larger validation sample (n=4,765 vs n=1,035), and provides an R² estimate (0.072) that is at least interpretable as model-level variance explained. Given the reduced covariate-leakage risk and stronger external evaluation context, PGS002247 is better supported overall.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Multiple myeloma”, trait_efo both plasma cell myeloma), same method (genome-wide significant variants) and same variant count (23) with EUR-only GWAS/EVAL. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC difference (0.644 in PGS002281 vs 0.69 in PGS002306) is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator, especially since covariates differ/are unclear. PGS002281 has clearer covariate disclosure (age, sex, geographic region) and provides an additional effect-size style metric (OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18), whereas PGS002306 lists covariates as unknown and lacks supporting OR/HR metrics. Given near-clone status and weak metric comparability, the better-supported metadata package is PGS002281.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable. Still, PGS002281 comes from a disease-focused multiple-myeloma risk prediction paper and shows stronger validation evidence on the visible fields: higher reported AUROC (0.644 vs 0.547) with similarly light covariates (age/sex/region vs age/sex/PCs/batch) and a stronger stratification metric (OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18 vs PGS000652 OR top 1% vs rest 2.6 with very wide CI crossing 1). PGS000652 is from a broad cancer PRS repository framework and its effect-size evidence is only modest (OR per SD 1.24). Overall support favors PGS002281.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (3,377), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same validation N (2,738), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC). PGS000083 is the better-supported choice for the broad target trait “pancreatic carcinoma” because its endpoint is a general pancreatic cancer diagnosis (trait_efo: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping: incident pancreatic cancer) and it is evaluated in a clearly reported European validation context (EVAL EUR 100%) with a very large validation sample (n=391,491) and an interpretable PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.49). PGS000794 is the better-supported choice for the broad target “pancreatic carcinoma” because its endpoint is a general pancreatic cancer diagnosis (trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident pancreatic cancer) and it is evaluated in a clearly specified EUR population with very large validation (n=391,491) and a PRS effect size reported (HR=1.49). In contrast, PGS002264 targets the narrower subtype pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (less directly aligned to the umbrella carcinoma target) and its reported AUROC=0.83 is a full/clinical model metric with explicit clinical-risk packaging and diabetes-related covariates (DM onset/age at DM diagnosis, family history), with evaluation ancestry not reported—making its performance less comparable as a standalone PRS. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the decision rests on endpoint breadth/clarity and covariate comparability, favoring PGS000794.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = malignant neoplasm of ovary; trait_efo = ovarian neoplasm), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), identical training cohort (UKB) and training/validation sample sizes, and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. Given this near-clone setup, PGS000551 has slightly stronger reported discrimination/evidence in the selected validation record (higher full-model AUROC 0.558 vs 0.546; higher Nagelkerke R² 0.00819 vs 0.00676; slightly higher per-SD OR 1.234 vs 1.207), while PGS000558’s main advantage is method/scale (lassosum with ~1.1M variants vs P+T with 12 variants) but without corresponding better observed performance here. Therefore PGS000551 is better-supported on the visible empirical metrics, though confidence is only moderate because both rely on full-model (not PRS-only) metrics and differences are small.

PGS000903 is better supported as a standalone Parkinson disease PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis (multiple PD consortia/cohorts listed) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and provides multiple performance signals (full-model AUROC/R² plus a strong risk gradient OR top vs bottom quartile=6.25). PGS003763 is a much sparser 44-SNP genome-wide-significant score with no training/development details and only an HR (high vs low tertile=1.72) from an incident PD time-to-event framing, which is less directly comparable for generic PD risk and offers weaker evidence of PRS strength despite its large evaluation N. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the broader disease-focused evidence package and stronger effect-size gradient favor PGS000903.

Both candidates align to Parkinson disease (same trait_reported/trait_efo), but PGS000902 is better supported as a standalone PD genetic risk score: it comes from a large disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis with explicit multi-cohort training/development (23andMe, IPDGC, UKB, etc.) and a larger GWAS-hit set (90 variants vs 44). PGS003763 is embedded in a frailty-focused incident-PD study context and provides only a tertile HR (1.72) without PRS-comparable AUC/R2 or clear training/development details (samples_training N/A, no cohorts listed), making its PRS evidence package thinner despite a large evaluation N. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, and PGS000902’s reported AUROC is full-model, but its overall disease-genetics study archetype and richer development metadata outweigh PGS003763’s single HR summary.

Both candidates target the same disease concept (trait_reported Pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and use the same sparse GWAS-hits construction (22 genome-wide significant variants), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either record—so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. Given that, PGS000083 has the stronger overall support: it uses a direct incident pancreatic cancer endpoint (vs PGS000663’s horizon-conditioned 0–10 years follow-up packaging, which is a weaker generic-disease match) and it is validated at vastly larger scale (n=391,491 vs n=956), with a stronger reported full-model discrimination (AUROC/C-index ~0.74 vs AUROC 0.67) and slightly stronger per-SD effect size signal (HR 1.49 vs OR 1.44). PGS000663 also includes more clinically entangled covariates (e.g., diabetic status, fasting status, waist-to-hip ratio) alongside the horizon framing, further reducing comparability. Overall, PGS000083 is better-supported on endpoint fidelity and validation context.

PGS000725 is the better-supported choice for the broad target “pancreatic carcinoma” because its endpoint is a general pancreatic cancer diagnosis (trait_reported: Pancreatic cancer; phenotyping_reported: Incident Pancreatic cancer; trait_efo: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) with clean/basic covariate handling (genotyping array only), making its reported discrimination less likely to be covariate-inflated. In contrast, PGS002264 targets a specific subtype (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma) and its high full-model AUROC (0.83) is paired with explicit heavy clinical-risk packaging covariates (diabetes onset/age at DM diagnosis, waist circumference, and first-degree family history), with no PGS-only metrics reported—so the apparent performance advantage is not interpretable as PRS strength. Although PGS002264 uses more variants (49 vs 22), the covariate leakage/packaging concern and narrower endpoint reduce its support relative to the cleaner, more directly comparable PGS000725.

PGS003763 is better supported for the generic target of Parkinson disease because it has strong endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported = incident Parkinson Disease) with clean/basic covariates (array + 10 PCs) and much broader evaluation support (EUR, n=314,998) plus a solid PRS effect size (HR high vs low tertile 1.72). PGS001353 is also on-target but is a very sparse 6-variant score evaluated only in Asian ancestry (n=25,646) and its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index 0.63 with a relatively heavy epidemiologic covariate set, making the metric less PRS-comparable; its HR (top vs bottom tertile 1.81) is similar but not enough to offset the much weaker structural/validation support.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to Parkinson disease (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported match). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so candidate_b’s full-model C-index=0.63 is not a comparable standalone PRS metric, especially given its heavier covariate set (education, BMI, dialect, etc.), making the discrimination harder to attribute to the PRS. Candidate_a, while smaller validation (n=786 vs n=25,646), uses cleaner/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs) and includes more GWAS-significant variants (16 vs 6), providing a more plausible standalone PRS construction for the target trait on the visible fields. Ancestry-wise they target different populations (EUR vs Asian), but with no deployment ancestry specified, the cleaner PRS evidence package favors PGS000123.

PGS003763 and PGS000123 both align well to the target (Parkinson disease; EUR GWAS/EVAL; basic covariates only). Neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we fall back to endpoint/context and effect-size strength. PGS003763 is evaluated on a far larger incident PD cohort (n=314,998) and reports a clear risk gradient (HR high vs low tertile = 1.72, 95% CI 1.54–1.93), providing stronger, more interpretable PRS signal evidence than PGS000123’s small validation (n=786) with less directly comparable metrics (p-value and a beta without clear PRS-only discrimination context). Variant count is also higher for PGS003763 (44 vs 16), supporting better polygenic capture within the same GWAS-hits method family.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to Parkinson disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and both use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), with no obvious clinical-risk packaging. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC in PGS000902 (0.651) cannot be treated as a clean PRS-comparable advantage over PGS000123. However, PGS000902 is better supported structurally and by study archetype: it is derived from a large, disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis (Lancet Neurol; multiple PD consortia/biobanks listed) and uses many more genome-wide significant variants (90 vs 16), which is a positive within-method signal. PGS000123 has weaker overall support: no training/development cohort information, fewer variants, and only association/effect-size reporting without discrimination metrics. Overall, PGS000902 has the stronger evidence package despite lacking PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease) and neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R², so performance comparability is limited. PGS000903 is better supported structurally and by study context: it is a disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis score (23andMe, IPDGC, UKB, etc.) with far broader development/transport context and a much richer polygenic model (1805 variants, C+T) than PGS000123’s 16 genome-wide significant variants with no listed training/development cohorts. While PGS000903’s reported AUROC=0.692 and R²=0.054 are full-model (covariates include age/sex/PCs) and thus not PRS-comparable, it at least provides additional discrimination evidence (e.g., OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25) under basic covariates, whereas PGS000123 reports only association p-value/beta without discrimination metrics. Overall, PGS000903 has the stronger evidence package; confidence is moderate because neither record reports PRS-only metrics and PGS000903’s key metrics are full-model.

Both candidates target the same disease concept (trait_efo: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; trait_reported: Pancreatic cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator. PGS000663 is better supported on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it is from a pancreatic-cancer risk-prediction paper and uses a defined horizon phenotype ("Pancreatic cancer (0–10 years of follow-up)") with a straightforward GWAS-hits construction (22 genome-wide significant variants) and an OR per SD of 1.44. PGS000794 comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration framework and explicitly includes family history of cancer among covariates, making its higher full-model AUROC (0.745) more likely covariate-driven and less comparable to standalone PRS performance; it also re-weights an older 22-variant score rather than presenting a direct disease-focused construction. Overall, PGS000663 has the cleaner disease-specific evidence package, while PGS000794’s apparent metric advantage is discounted due to pan-cancer packaging and family-history augmentation.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis, target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease), use the same basic covariates (PCs 1–5, age, sex), and have the same training scale and validation sample size (n=999), so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate them. Given otherwise near-identical context, these extra performance/effect-size fields and higher-coverage score make PGS000903 better-supported.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept (peripheral vascular disease) because it targets the clinically close and well-defined endpoint peripheral artery disease with an incident PAD phenotype, comes from a disease-focused PAD/MALE study, and provides stronger PRS-relevant evidence via a substantial per-SD effect size (HR=1.66) plus a basic covariate set (age/sex/PCs) and broad multi-ancestry evaluation (n=304,294). PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite not having PRS-only AUC/R2: it targets a closely aligned and clinically specific endpoint (incident peripheral artery disease, a core manifestation within peripheral vascular disease) and comes from a disease-focused study with broad multi-cohort development and large multi-ancestry evaluation (validation n=304,294 across multiple ancestries). It also reports a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.66), which is meaningful evidence of discriminative signal. In contrast, PGS001843 is from a UKB portability/framework paper with a vague/unspecified phenotype (“peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”), sparse model (242 variants) and only a very small partial correlation (0.0151) as performance evidence, with much smaller validation (n=19,668). Overall, endpoint fidelity + study archetype + effect-size support favor PGS005217 over the framework-style, weak-metric PGS001843.

PGS003586 has clearly better endpoint fidelity to the target trait preeclampsia: its phenotyping_reported is “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia” and trait_reported matches, whereas PGS004593’s phenotyping_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” a related but non-identical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model discrimination is not a strong differentiator. Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (schizophrenia), same method (PRS-CS), same covariates (basic demographics/PCs/batch/platform), same GWAS/EVAL ancestry pattern (mostly EUR GWAS; EUR eval), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). PGS001307 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.638 (with CI) and PGS-only R2=0.0238 under basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and the R2 is plausibly below the ulcerative colitis liability h2 ceiling noted in the context. PGS002066 has cleaner endpoint wording (non–time-to-event) and a stronger structural method/coverage signal (LDpred2 with 566k variants, larger training N), but it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and only provides a full-model AUROC=0.57 with unknown covariates plus a weak/uncertain OR=1.11 (CI crosses 1), making its PRS contribution hard to judge. Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Type 2 Diabetes), same publication and release date, identical ancestry distribution, identical training cohort (UKB) and training/validation sample sizes, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R² reported, so metrics are weak differentiators). With covariates listed as 0 for both, the only visible separation is that PGS004052 has marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.6371 vs 0.6360), R² (0.05548 vs 0.05494), and slightly higher OR per SD (1.6477 vs 1.6442). Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match bladder cancer), identical basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (so full-model AUROC differences are essentially noise). PGS000613 is better supported by stronger risk stratification (OR top 1% vs rest 2.91 vs 1.47 for PGS000610) and slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.301 vs 1.292), plus larger training and validation sample sizes. PGS000610’s marginally higher full-model AUROC/R2 does not compensate given both are full-model metrics with the same covariates and near-identical values.

Both candidates target ulcerative colitis with identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported and come from the same UKB portability paper with similar ancestry evaluation mixes, so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so candidate_b’s full-model AUROC=0.57 is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage, especially with covariates listed as Unknown. However, with PRS-only metrics absent for both, structural signals dominate: PGS002066 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (566,637 vs 1,505 for PGS001855’s penalized sparse regression), which is generally better aligned with capturing polygenic signal for complex disease. Candidate_a’s only performance evidence is a modest partial-r (0.0625) without effect sizes, while candidate_b at least provides an OR estimate (1.11, albeit weak). Overall, PGS002066 has the stronger methodological/coverage support in this near-clone comparison.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (bladder cancer / urinary bladder carcinoma), same phenotyping_reported (Cancer of bladder), same method (GWAS Hits) with the same 13 variants, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not clean PRS-comparable). With endpoints and structure essentially identical, the small full-model AUROC difference (0.567 for PGS000611 vs 0.572 for PGS000610) is likely noise; instead, PGS000611 has stronger risk stratification evidence (OR top 1% vs rest 2.66 vs 1.47) and larger training/validation sample sizes (12,992 train; 13,530 eval vs 7,469 train; 7,622 eval), making it marginally better supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target urinary bladder cancer: identical trait_reported/trait_efo, identical phenotyping_reported (“Cancer of bladder”), same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same EUR-only ancestry context, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics are shown, so AUROC differences are weak evidence). Candidate_b (PGS000612) has a trivially higher full-model AUROC/R2 (0.572/0.013 vs 0.567/0.0114), but it has weaker risk stratification evidence (top 1% OR 1.47 with wide CI crossing 1 vs 2.66 with CI clearly >1 for PGS000611) and a smaller training/validation scale (7,469/7,622 vs 12,992/13,530). Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the stronger top-tail OR and slightly larger support favor PGS000611, but the overall difference is small, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones for urinary bladder cancer: same trait_reported/trait_efo, identical phenotyping_reported (“Cancer of bladder”), identical EUR-only ancestry across GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and size (n=7,469), same validation size (n=7,622), same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and identical reported performance/effect sizes (full-model AUROC 0.572; Nagelkerke R² 0.013; OR per SD 1.292; no PGS-only AUC/R² for either). With metrics and endpoint fidelity indistinguishable, the only differentiator is method_name: PGS000612 uses Pruning+Thresholding (P+T), which is at least a tuned PRS construction approach versus PGS000610’s “GWAS Hits” label. Given otherwise identical evidence, PGS000612 is marginally better supported structurally, but the decision is low-confidence due to the effective tie.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported bladder cancer; EFO urinary bladder carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. PGS000723 has better endpoint fidelity via an explicit disease-incidence definition (phenotyping_reported: incident bladder cancer) and is supported by a large multi-cohort, disease-focused development context (many named cohorts; eval n=400,812), whereas PGS000611 comes from a repository-style UKB-only setup (Cancer PRSweb; training/dev/ eval all UKB EUR) with a less specific phenotype label (“Cancer of bladder”). Given similar sparse GWS-variant methods and variant counts (14 vs 13), the stronger study archetype/transportability context and clearer incident endpoint make PGS000723 better supported overall.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported Bladder cancer; trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are weak evidence. PGS000723 has slightly better endpoint fidelity via an explicit disease-incidence definition (phenotyping_reported: "Incident bladder cancer") and is supported by a large external evaluation sample (n=400,812) across many contributing cohorts, suggesting broader transportability than PGS000610’s single-cohort MGI development/evaluation (training n=7,469; validation n=7,622). PGS000610 does provide additional effect-size metrics and basic covariates, but its evidence package is narrower and its full-model AUROC (0.572) is slightly lower than PGS000723 (0.583) with no PRS-only metrics to counterbalance the much stronger multi-cohort evaluation context of PGS000723.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint is a direct disease diagnosis match (trait_efo=urolithiasis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=Urinary calculus) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very broad variant coverage (731,196), plus it is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS), supporting portability. PGS001250 does provide clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.5668; PGS-only R² 0.00592), but it comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very small SNP set (341) and a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for generic urolithiasis risk. Given the framework+sparsity+TTE penalties versus PGS002075’s closer endpoint and stronger structural properties, PGS002075 wins despite lacking PRS-only AUROC/R².

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Urinary calculus/urolithiasis), same UKB portability publication, same training cohort and size (UKB; n=391,124), same covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), same validation size (n=19,913) and ancestry distribution, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS002075 shows a higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (731,196 vs 5,599), which is a favorable structural signal for a complex disease when other fields are identical. PGS001864’s sparse penalized regression score has weaker partial-r and much lower variant count with no compensating performance evidence.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint mapping is directly aligned (trait_efo=urolithiasis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=Urinary calculus) and it comes with broader evaluation evidence across multiple ancestries (EVAL includes AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS with 8 performance records), which is supportive for transportability beyond EUR. Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (PGS000723 0.583 vs PGS000613 0.571) is not a reliable differentiator, especially with different covariates. PGS000613 has cleaner, more standard adjustment (age/sex/PCs/batch) and provides additional PRS-relevant evidence (OR per SD 1.301 and top-1% OR 2.91 plus pseudo-R²), whereas PGS000723 reports only AUROC with minimal supporting effect-size/other-metric context and uses only genotyping array as covariate. Endpoint-wise, PGS000723’s 'incident bladder cancer' is slightly narrower than PGS000613’s generic 'cancer of bladder' for a generic disease-risk target. Overall, PGS000613 is better supported on the visible fields.

PGS004493 has tighter endpoint fidelity to urolithiasis via an explicit ICD code phenotype (N20 calculus of kidney and ureter) and provides a PRS-discrimination signal (OR=1.23 per SD), whereas PGS001864 comes from a portability framework paper and only reports a weak partial correlation (partial-r=0.032) with no AUC/R2 or effect size. Although PGS001864 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and known basic covariates, its framework archetype plus weaker performance evidence makes it less supported than the more disease-endpoint-specific LDpred2 score in PGS004493.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported, same basic covariates, EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same publication/date, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 so full-model AUROC differences are essentially noise). With endpoints and design effectively tied, PGS000613 has the more supportive secondary evidence: larger training sample (12,992 vs 7,469), larger validation sample (13,530 vs 7,622), slightly more variants (15 vs 13), and notably stronger risk stratification in the reported top-1% OR (2.91 [1.99–4.24] vs 1.47 [0.779–2.77], where PGS000612 is weak/uncertain). Therefore PGS000613 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS004563 is better supported for the target urolithiasis because its endpoint is a specific ICD diagnosis code for kidney/ureter stones (phenotyping_reported: N20), which is a direct clinical instantiation of urolithiasis/nephrolithiasis, and it provides a PRS effect size (OR=1.283 per SD) giving at least some discriminative evidence. In contrast, PGS001864 comes from a UKB portability framework paper (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) and only reports a weak partial correlation (partial-r=0.0323) with no OR/HR/AUC/R2, making its PRS signal harder to trust despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation. Both are UKB-derived and lack clean PRS-only AUC/R2, but the disease-focused risk-factor/disease metaPRS framing plus the available OR favors PGS004563 over the framework portability score PGS001864.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the target trait urolithiasis because its phenotype mapping is directly coherent with the target (trait_efo=urolithiasis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=Urinary calculus) and it provides at least one PRS-comparable performance signal (partial correlation partial-r=0.0385 with CI) plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS), which is supportive for transportability. In contrast, PGS004563 targets a closely related but not identical mapped trait (trait_efo=nephrolithiasis) and appears to be a risk-factor metaPRS integration framework (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with unknown covariates and only a single OR=1.283 (moderate/weak) and no PRS-only AUC/R2 or other comparable metrics; its evaluation is EUR-only. Overall, PGS002075 has cleaner endpoint alignment to urolithiasis and more informative validation context than PGS004563.

PGS000723 is better supported overall for urinary bladder cancer because it has stronger endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported: incident bladder cancer vs PGS000612’s broader “Cancer of bladder”) and a much broader, multi-cohort development context (many named cohorts including deCODE) with a very large evaluation sample (n=400,812 vs n=7,622). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.583 vs 0.572) is weak evidence; however, PGS000723’s covariate set (genotyping array) is at least as clean as PGS000612’s age/sex/PCs/batch, and PGS000612’s main extra evidence is effect sizes (OR per SD ~1.29) without a PRS-only metric. Taken together, the incident endpoint plus broader external-style cohort backing makes PGS000723 the more reliable pick.

PGS000541 is the better-supported uterine cancer PRS: it matches the target trait directly (trait_efo uterine cancer; phenotyping_reported malignant neoplasm of uterus) and provides substantially richer evaluation evidence (full-model AUROC 0.576 with CI, Nagelkerke R², Brier score, and OR top 1% vs rest) with clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs). PGS003740 is close in endpoint (corpus uteri / uterine corpus cancer) but is from a pan-cancer prognostic framing, has much smaller training and validation samples (n=698 train; n=372 eval), unknown covariates, and reports only a single per-SD OR without any discrimination/calibration metrics, making it less well evidenced on the visible fields.

PGS001864 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target “urolithiasis”: its trait_efo is exactly urolithiasis and phenotyping_reported is a direct diagnosis-style “Urinary calculus,” whereas PGS001250 is specifically “Calculus of kidney and ureter (time-to-event)” with trait_efo mapped to nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis and a TTE endpoint (a noted mismatch risk for a generic disease target). Both are UKB framework-style scores, but PGS001864 uses a genome-wide penalized regression with many more variants (5599 vs 341), which is a favorable structural signal versus the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001250. Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.5668/0.00592), those metrics are modest and do not outweigh the stronger phenotype alignment plus less-sparse construction of PGS001864; PGS001864’s partial-r (0.0323) provides at least some PRS-only signal despite lacking AUROC/R².

PGS001250 has clear endpoint alignment to urolithiasis (ICD-style “Calculus of kidney and ureter” with nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis EFO) and, critically, reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5668 and PGS-only R² 0.00592) with basic covariates, plus broader multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) which supports transportability evidence. PGS004563 matches the ICD code label (N20) but provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R² at all (only an OR=1.283, which is modest) and has unknown covariates and EUR-only evaluation, leaving substantially weaker visible support despite its larger variant count and newer release.

Both candidates are near-clones: same uterine cancer endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported match), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same UKB training cohort and training N=7,131, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation N=6,987; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R2, which are not clean PRS-comparable). With endpoints and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS000541 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.576 vs 0.572), slightly higher pseudo-R² (0.0133 vs 0.0126), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.311 vs 1.302), while PGS000542 only has a higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.6 vs 2.12). Given the minimal, mixed differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, I pick PGS000541 on the marginally stronger overall discrimination signals, but confidence is low.

PGS000542 is better supported for the target “uterine cancer” because its endpoint mapping is directly aligned (trait_efo=uterine cancer; phenotyping_reported=Malignant neoplasm of uterus) and it provides a richer, cleaner evaluation package (AUROC reported as 0.572 with CI plus pseudo-R², Brier score, and multiple effect-size summaries) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch), reducing concerns about clinical-risk packaging. PGS003740 is close in phenotype (uterine corpus cancer / Corpus Uteri) but comes from a pan-cancer prognostic framing, has unknown covariates, much smaller training/validation (n=698 train; n=372 eval), and reports only a single OR without any discrimination/R² metrics, leaving weaker visible evidence overall.

PGS001536 is endpoint-faithful to vitiligo (trait_reported vitiligo time-to-event; phenotyping_reported “TTE vitiligo”) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates only and an R2 well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is “anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients,” which is treatment-induced and not vitiligo, and it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only an HR and a meta-analysis p-value). Despite PGS001536 coming from a pan-trait UKB framework paper, the strong endpoint coherence plus explicit PRS-only metrics outweigh PGS000760’s off-target endpoint and missing comparable metrics.

PGS001536 is better supported on PRS-relevant evidence: it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.64193; PGS R² 0.01621) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, array), and has clear training context (UKB; n=269,704) plus multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). Its PRS-only R² is also well below the vitiligo h2_obs ceiling (~0.174), so it passes the sanity check. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/phenotype incoherence (phenotyping_reported = "Red hair" despite trait_reported/EFO = vitiligo), lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² (only a pseudo R²/full-model-style metric shown), and has no training sample information, making its support weaker despite the disease-focused publication framing.

PGS001795 is a direct uterine cancer/uterine carcinoma endpoint match (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both “Uterine cancer”) and provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) with basic demographic/PC covariates; its PRS-only R2 is also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; liability h2≈0.0116). It is developed in a large multi-biobank global PRS framework using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) and evaluated on a much larger EUR validation sample (n=170,276). In contrast, PGS003740 targets the narrower “uterine corpus cancer” concept (“Corpus Uteri”), uses only 16 genome-wide significant SNPs, has unknown covariates and no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported (only an OR=1.38), and is supported by a very small training (n=698) and validation (n=372) context, making its evidence package materially weaker overall.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity to the target (candidate_a: “Malignant neoplasm of uterus” with trait_efo uterine cancer; candidate_b: “Uterine cancer” with trait_efo uterine carcinoma, a near-synonym). Candidate_b provides a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.001948; Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out), whereas candidate_a reports only full-model AUROC/R2 (AUROC=0.572) which is not directly comparable as PRS-only evidence. Structurally, candidate_b uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with ~912k variants versus candidate_a’s P+T with 20 variants, which is generally better suited for polygenic signal capture. Although candidate_b comes from a global biobank framework-style paper and has heavier basic covariates, it also has much larger European evaluation (n=170,276 vs 6,987) and its PRS-only R2 is plausible under the trait heritability ceiling, making it the better-supported record overall compared with candidate_a’s sparse score and non-PRS-only performance reporting.

PGS001795 is better supported as a standalone PRS for uterine cancer because it reports a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.001948; “Nagelkerke’s R2 covariates regressed out”), whereas PGS000541 reports only full-model metrics (AUROC=0.576, pseudo-R2=0.0133) that are not directly comparable as PRS-only performance. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (phenotyping_reported matches uterine cancer/uterus malignancy), with PGS001795’s trait_reported also directly “Uterine cancer.” Structurally, PGS001795 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto) with ~912k variants versus PGS000541’s 18-variant GWAS-hits score, which is generally weaker for polygenic signal capture. Although PGS001795 comes from a global biobank framework-style paper and has heavier basic covariates, it still provides cleaner PRS-isolated performance evidence than PGS000541, whose apparent performance is largely covariate-driven and lacks PRS-only metrics.

PGS001795 is the better-supported choice for the target uterine cancer because it has exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Uterine cancer”, EFO uterine carcinoma) and provides a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) that is at least interpretable as PRS signal. Although it comes from a global biobank framework paper, it uses only basic demographic/PC covariates and a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage, and its PRS-only R2 is consistent with the very low heritability ceiling noted for uterine cancer. In contrast, PGS000786 is for endometrial cancer (a close but not exact match) and its reported discrimination is dominated by a covariate-heavy integrated risk model (includes family history and multiple reproductive/hormonal/BMI factors) with no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its higher full-model AUROC/R2 largely non-comparable for judging standalone PRS quality.

PGS000738 is better supported for the target trait vitiligo because its supporting publication is explicitly about autoimmune vitiligo and polygenic inheritance, whereas PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported is "anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients," a treatment-induced, therapy-specific endpoint that is not vitiligo and signals endpoint mismatch/clinical-context packaging. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS000738 at least reports a (full-model) pseudo R² and beta in a vitiligo-focused context, while PGS000760 provides only an HR and a meta-analysis p-value tied to the non-vitiligo phenotype. Both are EUR-only, so ancestry doesn’t differentiate; the decision is driven primarily by endpoint fidelity and study focus favoring PGS000738 despite its noisy phenotyping_reported field.

PGS000542 is the better-supported choice for the target trait uterine cancer because its endpoint is directly aligned (trait_efo=uterine cancer; phenotyping_reported=Malignant neoplasm of uterus) and its evaluation uses only basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), making the reported discrimination less confounded by clinical risk-factor packaging. With both candidates lacking PRS-only AUC/R², the cleaner phenotype match and cleaner covariate context favor PGS000542 despite PGS000786’s larger validation sample and higher full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clones: same T2D endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (23,748), same ancestry distribution and evaluation setup, same covariates field (0), and same validation sample size (90,274). PGS000541 is the better-supported match to the target trait uterine cancer on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is exactly "uterine cancer" and phenotyping_reported is "Malignant neoplasm of uterus," whereas PGS000786 targets "Endometrial cancer" with trait_efo "endometrial carcinoma" (a close/dominant subtype but still not the umbrella uterine cancer label). PGS003740 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (uterine cancer) on endpoint fidelity and PRS signal: its trait/phenotyping are directly aligned to uterine corpus cancer (“Corpus Uteri”, EFO uterine corpus cancer) and it reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.38, 95% CI 1.20–1.58) without relying on an explicitly covariate-heavy risk-factor package. PGS001250 is better supported on the visible fields: it provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5668 and PGS-only R² 0.00592, with CI) under basic covariates, and it has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) even though the selected record is EUR. Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for urolithiasis/nephrolithiasis (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are ICD-10 N20; same EFO), come from the same publication, and have the same EUR-only training/validation context (UKB; n=174,489 train; n=56,192 eval) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, so metrics cannot differentiate. Although PGS004493 uses LDpred2 (a strong single-score shrinkage method), PGS004563’s meta/ensemble-style method label (RFDiseasemetaPRS) is structurally compatible with multi-score aggregation and, combined with the stronger OR, makes it better-supported on the available fields.
